bio.en: Maggie Crowley is VP of Product at Toast and has held product leadership roles at Charlie Health, Drift, BevSpot, and TripAdvisor.
bio.zh: 玛吉·克劳利（Maggie Crowley）是 Toast 的产品副总裁，曾在 Charlie Health、Drift、BevSpot 和 TripAdvisor 担任产品领导职务。

summary.en: Maggie argues that when you catch yourself saying "that's not my job," it's usually exactly what you should do to move faster. She describes the PM as the emotional center of the team, responsible for keeping everyone motivated and optimistic. The episode is full of grounded advice on ownership, scrappiness, and doing whatever it takes to ship.
summary.zh: 玛吉认为，当你忍不住说"那不是我的活儿"时，那往往恰恰是你应该去做、从而更快推进的事。她把 PM 描述成团队的"情绪中心"，负责让大家保持动力与乐观。本期充满了关于主人翁意识、灵活务实以及"为交付不遗余力"的扎实建议。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: If you ever find yourself saying something like, that's not my job, that's probably a thing you should do. And you know what? It probably isn't your job and it probably is someone else's job and you can spend your life getting frustrated at that or you can just get over and get the work done. And people who are willing to just get the work done will move faster. Their products will be more successful and they probably aren't carrying around all that anger and crappy emotion because as a PM, for better or for worse, and maybe this is not how we all want it to be, but you're oftentimes the emotional center of the team and it's your job to keep people motivated, keep people excited, keep them bought into the project, and you just have to keep that optimism going and it's hard work and part of it can be just like, you know what? Let me take that on. I'll do this thing. I'll hop on this sales call, I'll implement this with the customer. You just have to do whatever it takes.
turns.zh: 如果你发现自己总在说"这不是我的工作"之类的话，那很可能这件事你应该去做。知道吗？这确实可能不是你的工作，而是别人的职责。你要么终日为此感到沮丧，要么就放下架子，把工作完成。那些愿意埋头工作的团队成员，往往能进展得更快。他们的产品更易获得成功，而且他们可能不会被负面情绪所困扰。因为作为产品经理，无论是好是坏，也许这并非我们都乐见的局面，但你往往是团队的情绪核心，你的职责是激励大家，保持他们的热情，让他们全身心投入项目。你必须始终保持乐观，这是一项艰巨的任务。有时你得主动承担责任：我来接这个销售电话吧，我来和客户一起实施这个方案吧。但关键是，你必须不择手段地把工作完成。

turns.zh: 您在播客、博客、推特上发布了大量内容，我相信还有很多我没见过的。所以我做了件事，就是尽可能仔细浏览了您的所有内容，寻找我们今天可以深入探讨的话题。我觉得从如何成为一名成功的产品经理，以及成为一名成功的产品经理需要具备哪些条件说起会很有趣，特别是从职业生涯的长期角度来看。您与很多产品经理合作过，也招聘过很多产品经理，还管理过许多产品经理，所以我想问的问题是，您在最优秀的产品经理身上看到的共同特质是什么？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah, it's an interesting question mostly because I've worked in startups, zero to one, scaling stage startups, enterprise, all that kind of stuff. And there's a lot of content out there I think on how those roles are different and how PMs are different across those different types of companies. But what I've seen is that there are some standard things that are the same across the role no matter whether you're a consumer, B2B or startup or a large company and in particular about what sets PMs apart from one another. And the things that I look for when I'm hiring or when I'm looking to promote people or when PMs stand out, even when you're not looking are three things. (00:05:31): First, I think the best PMs are really good at breaking things down and simplifying things. So, finding at any moment what is the really truly the only thing you need to do, especially in a big company, there are 8 million priorities, there's 700 OKRs, there's 25,000 projects you could work on, and teams will get bogged down in that complexity. Similarly speaking at a startup, you might think that it's easy to find the one thing to do, but at the same time there's so many fires that are happening and so many things you could do in such a world of opportunity that even just picking one and sticking with it is really difficult. And so the best PMs not only can find the one thing to work on, but they can stay with that one thing long enough to actually finish it.
turns.zh: 是的，这是一个很有趣的问题，主要是因为我曾在初创公司工作过，从零到一，再到扩张阶段的初创公司，还有企业公司等等。关于这些不同类型的公司中产品经理角色的差异，以及产品经理的不同之处，我认为有很多相关内容。但我发现，无论您是在消费者领域、B2B领域、初创公司还是大型公司，产品经理这个角色都有一些不变的标准特质，特别是区分不同产品经理的特质。当我招聘或晋升员工时，或者当产品经理表现出色时，即使他们自己没有主动表现，我也会关注三个方面。（00:05:31）：首先，我认为最优秀的产品经理都非常善于拆解问题并化繁为简。无论何时，都能找到真正需要做的那件事，特别是在大公司里，优先级有八百万个，OKR有700个，项目有25000个，团队很容易被复杂的环境拖累。同样，在初创公司里，你可能会觉得找出那件要紧事很容易，但同时也面临着诸多紧急任务和大量可做之事。在这样的机会丛林中，能选定一件事并坚持到底真的很难。因此，最优秀的产品经理不仅能找到要做的那件事，还能长期专注于此并最终完成它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's a really interesting point, because it sounds simple. Also, just this idea of simplifying, but I think there's so much up there partly because within simplifying is prioritizing and you can almost boil down the job of the PM as they're just prioritizing and telling people what is next. And so I think that's a really powerful point you're making.
turns.zh: 我觉得这点很值得深思，因为这听起来很简单。还有，关于化繁为简的概念，但我认为这里面有很深的奥义，简化其实就是优先排序。可以把产品经理的工作归结为优先排序和告诉团队下一步该做什么。所以我觉得您提出的观点非常有价值。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Prioritization is a tough word because there's so much wrapped up in that and what it means to prioritize. And I've worked for people who wanted to understand the formula for prioritization and why this thing and how can you prove that this is the right thing to work on and not that thing. And then a week goes by and then they want to reevaluate the priority and they want to re-litigate the priority. And so it's so much more than just a moment in time deciding, but it's the ability to stay with it and to make sure that it continues to be the most important thing, that you finish it and actually see that it works and that you can get people to continue to stay excited and engaged in that project. (00:07:13): Because I think a lot of when we talk about product, it's like, oh, what should you build? What should you ship? But then you actually have to ship that and that can take a week, a month, three months, six months, a year. And so as a PM, your job is to stay on that and be the person who's beating that drum over and over again, and the best PMs are the ones who can do that and have the resilience and the energy to stay with it.
turns.zh:
优先排序是个棘手的词汇，因为它涵盖了太多层面，也蕴含着深刻的含义。我曾为一些希望理解优先排序公式的人工作，他们总想知道为什么要优先处理某件事，又该如何证明这个决策是正确的。但一周过去后，他们又想重新评估优先级，再次争论这个问题。因此，优先排序绝非一时之选，而是要坚持下去，确保它始终是最重要的事务，直至完成并验证其成效，还要持续激发团队对项目的热情。

（00:07:13）：因为谈及产品时，人们往往纠结于“该开发什么？该上线什么？”。但实际上，上线可能需要一周、一个月、三个月、六个月的时间。作为产品经理，你的职责是持续跟进，始终保持推动力，而优秀的产品经理必须具备这种韧性和耐力，才能始终如一地把事情做好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Energy. That's a really important part of that. I'm going to ask you how you suggest people get better at these things. So, either we can go into how you found you get better at simplifying or we go through all three and then we can come back, however you prefer.
turns.zh: 能量。这是至关重要的一点。接下来我想问问大家，如何才能在这方面有所提升。或者我们可以先快速过一遍三个要点，再深入探讨，按您的意愿安排。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Let's just do all three really quick and then we can dig in.
turns.zh: 那就快速过一遍三个要点吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds great.
turns.zh: 听起来不错。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: So, yeah, first one, simplifying. I think the second one has to do with this point about sticking with something and it's following up on results. So many people in the spec or the one pager or something will say, okay, here's the metric that I care about. Here's what I want to move. Awesome. Maybe they'll even write a SQL query, get a dashboard going, figure out what the number is today, that gets you some extra points, but the really, really good PMs remember to follow up. Because especially when you're in management, couple layers up in management, I'm not going to remember to follow up on that feature, but if a PM comes back to me and says, "Hey, remember we did that thing, here's what happened." I can't tell you how rare that is and how many times as a leader you might have to ask for that and for the people you don't have to ask that of is one of the best things when I'm looking at PMs and it's easy. (00:08:43): It's not hard to do that, especially if you've set up metric tracking or you know how to pull that information or you have somebody who can help you get that. It's pretty easy to do and it's really high value activity. And then the third thing, and I think maybe we'll talk about this later too, is that a phrase actually we were talking about David Cancel before we started carrying the water, and this was a big theme when I joined Drift, and this is about how you can't be a good PM if you're not willing to do the hard boring unglamorous work of customer support, sales, marketing, writing, copy, project management, you have to do that stuff. It's your job. No one else is going to do it, because at the end of the day, you're responsible for outcomes and results. So, you're the person that has to do that, and if you're willing to do that work, that's what's going to make your product successful, which is what makes you successful.
turns.zh: 好的，第一个要点是简化复杂问题。第二个要点是坚持到底并跟进结果。许多人在需求文档或单页计划中会写道：好的，我关注这个指标，推进这个目标。不错，也许他们甚至会写个SQL查询，搭建个仪表盘，看看当前数据，但真正优秀的产品经理会持续跟进。尤其是在管理层级较高的职位上，如果我不主动追踪某个功能，产品经理主动汇报：“记得我们做了这个事，结果如何？”这种汇报太难得了。作为领导者，如果你不必催促下属完成这些工作，那就是最棒的。（00:08:43）：这并不难做到，尤其是如果你已建立指标追踪系统、掌握数据提取技巧，或者有助手支持的话。这些都是低成本、高价值的工作。第三个要点——我们稍后再探讨——是关于客户支持、销售、市场、文案、项目管理等基础工作的价值。优秀的产品经理必须亲力亲为这些工作，没人能替代你，因为最终的成果由你负责。正因如此，你必须亲自承担这些工作。如果你愿意承担这些职责，产品才能成功，你自己才能成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's such an interesting list because when you ask most people what you need to get better at to become a great product manager, it's always communication skills, collaboration skills, vision, strategy, and it feels like these are input metrics to what it's normally what people think about.
turns.zh: 这份清单相当有趣，因为当你问大多数人要成为一名优秀的产品经理需要提升哪些能力时，他们的回答总是沟通技巧、协作能力、愿景和战略，而这些似乎都是人们通常认为的输入指标。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Those things to me, communication, super important, analytical ability, really, really important. The ability to look at a, especially if you're doing something that has a user experience component, the ability to look at that and understand if it's going to work and build up intuition around that, also really important. Those are things that I would see as sort of basics of the role. These are the things that make you great at the role and strategy to me, and hopefully we'll talk about strategy in a bit. It's one tiny slice. You do a strategy, but it's 5% of the work that you do. Yes, it's important because you want to get your strategy and you need to pick the right products, but at the end of the day, the person who has a good strategy will not be as successful as the PM who ships more stuff, gets more reps and has the ability to actually create impact. So, to me, you could be great at strategy, but if you're not good at this stuff and your stuff isn't getting out the door, you're never going to be that great at the job.
turns.zh: 对我而言，沟通能力至关重要，分析能力也同样重要。若你从事涉及用户体验的工作，能够审视产品并判断其可行性，并由此建立直觉，这一点也极为关键。这些在我看来都是该职位的基本要素。它们决定了你能否在这个岗位上表现出色，而战略能力对我而言只是其中一小部分。制定战略固然重要，但这仅占你工作的5%之多。诚然，制定合理的战略和选对产品至关重要，但归根结底，拥有出色战略能力的PM若不能推出更多产品、积累更多经验并真正创造价值，最终也不会比那些高产输出的PM更成功。因此，在我看来，即便你精通战略，若无法将成果落地，永远无法成为卓越的产品经理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And impact is the other one. Everyone's always like, what makes a great PM? Oh, drive a lot of impact. And again-
turns.zh: 另一个关键词是影响力。人们总说如何成为优秀的PM？“要创造重大影响力”。但他们从不解释具体方法。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: But they never say how.
turns.zh: 没错，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right, exactly.
turns.zh: 比如，“好，我们制定战略，创造影响力。”但当我刚入行时，听到这些建议却茫然无措。当时我满怀热情，觉得“影响力？好，我要创造影响力。”却发现现实与理想相差十万八千里。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: It's like, cool, let's do a strategy, let's have impact. Then when I was starting off as a PM, I was hearing this advice and reading about it and I was sitting there saying, awesome, I want to create impact. And I'm looking at my job thinking, now what? Yeah, impact. Let's do it. Where is it? How do I find it? Someone help me.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这种挑战。好，我们回到这三个核心要素。我很好奇，你是如何提升这些能力的？能否分享一个具体案例？比如，如何提升沟通能力？如何锻炼这种能力？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. Okay, so let's go back to these three and I'm curious just what you found helps you become better at these things and also just an example if you can share. So, say what's simplifying? How does one build that muscle?
turns.zh: 我期待听听你的见解。回到这三个要素，我很想了解你如何提升这些能力，以及能否分享具体案例。比如，如何提升沟通能力？如何锻炼这种能力？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: This is a tough one because some people, a broad generalization that I think comes up in things like when you're interviewing PMs for a job and you say things like are they a simplifier or are they complexifier? Do they make things complicated? And so some of it's a little bit of just who you are and how you think. But having said that, there's one tool that I use that I actually learned from my dad when I was in grade school, which is when you write something, for example, and a lot of what we do as PMs is written, when you write something, read it out loud, literally just read the thing you wrote out loud and half the time you'll realize it's way too complicated, it doesn't make sense. Or what happens is when someone comes to me and they say, okay, I'm working on this thing, check it out, can you read it? (00:12:10): I read it and then I put it down and I say, "What are you trying to say?" And 99% of the time they say, "Oh, users are really struggling with this problem. We found this in research and we think that the way to solve it's to do X", but that's not what the document says. And so my reaction is always, and if anyone who I've worked with is listening to this, they're going to laugh is always, "Just say that. Just say that thing. The thing that you said to me in conversation is the thing you should write." There's no reason why your pros in a document has to be a certain way. We're not in school. Our goal is to get things done. So, those are just some simple tricks that I've used to help simplify what I've already been working on. (00:12:54): And as for how to boil things down and really find the most important thing to do, which is another part of simplification, I think the best thing you can do is just get as many reps in as you can, have people review your work and listen to them. There's a thing that happens I think with PMs where you join a company and then all of a sudden it's like my boss doesn't know what they're doing and the highest paid person's opinion and the founder wants to swoop in and mess everything up, but those people had an insight on the market that you're in that made the company worth founding and they probably know more than you and so you might want to listen to them. And so find people who can review your work, listen to them and ask them to help you simplify.
turns.zh:
这是个棘手的问题，因为有些人——我觉得这种情况在面试产品经理时会很常见，比如你问他们是简化者还是复杂化者？他们是否把事情搞得过于复杂？所以这在某种程度上取决于你个人的性格和思维方式。不过说到这儿，我倒是从小学时父亲那里学到一个方法：当你写下某段文字时（比如我们产品经理常做的工作），读出声来——真的大声朗读一遍。很多时候你会发现内容太复杂，根本说不通。又比如有人找我看设计稿时，我读完后会问：“你想表达什么？” 99%的人会说：“用户在这方面遇到了难题，我们通过调研发现问题根源，觉得应该用X方式解决”，但设计稿里根本没体现这些逻辑。所以我的建议是，直接说你实际想说的。如果你曾与我共事过的人听到这番话一定会笑："就直接说嘛！直接把对话里说的话写下来就行了。" 文档里的专业术语没必要太书面化——我们又不是在上学，目标是把事情做成。这些都是我用来简化已有工作的简单技巧。  

至于如何提炼核心要点，即简化的另一层含义，我认为最好的方法就是多实践、多征求意见。产品经理常会遇到这样的情况：加入新公司后，突然发现老板啥都不懂，创始人又想亲自操刀毁掉成果，但这些人对市场有深刻洞察，正是他们的见解成就了公司。所以要多听取他们的意见，找到能帮你简化的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'll share a couple other things that came to mind as you were talking, because this is a very hard thing to teach and you kind of have to do it again and again and honestly, I have this one manager who taught me to simplify in my writing and strategy docs one-pagers and things like that, and I think that actually had a big impact on my newsletter success is learning just to strip down as much as you can and anything that isn't necessary. So, there's a couple things that I'll share real quick. One is there's this book I read called On Writing Well, that is one of the most impactful books for writing for me, and the whole book is like, I don't know, 20 chapters and every chapter is more things you should cut from your writing and they show all these examples of like, here's a before and here's an after. (00:14:18): And all these words were cut and nothing changed. They're completely necessary. So, I think that book can help and partly it's just like what is not necessary? You think all these adjectives are important. Another thing I found really helpful is the rule of thirds, I guess the rule of three, of just always having three. Try not to go beyond three when you're giving strategy bets or priorities or things like that. Just try to keep things under three.
turns.zh:
接下来，我想分享几个在你发言时突然想到的要点，因为这确实是很难传授的技能，你必须反复实践。说实话，我曾遇到一位经理，他教会我如何简化写作和策略文档（如一页纸提案等），这对我的新闻通讯成功起到了重要作用——学会尽可能删繁就简，剔除所有不必要的内容。接下来，我会快速分享几点心得。首先，我读过一本叫《On Writing Well》的书，它对我的写作影响最大。整本书分为约20个章节，每个章节都教你如何从作品中删减冗余内容，并通过前后对比的例子展示，删减后的文本毫无影响，完全必要。所以这本书确实很有帮助。另外，要注意哪些内容是非必要的？你可能觉得某些形容词很重要，但实际上它们可有可无。

还有一点我发现很管用，那就是“三分法”原则——策略建议、优先事项等内容最好控制在三个或以下。保持简洁明了即可。若有第四个要点，需想办法整合进去。四个要点看起来会显得凌乱不整洁。

是的，我完全认同这种商学院前顾问的观点：任何列表都应控制在三个或更少，绝不超过三个。要保持数字整齐，若有第四个要点，需想办法巧妙整合。

没错，我也曾犯过超过三个要点的错误，但现在努力避免了。

你用的Notion平台，三个要点下有子项目，但至少结构清晰。

没错。还有一点，关键是要专注于最重要的内容。人们常想把一堆想法堆在一起，但这样只会冲淡整体效果。应该选取最具影响力的核心内容，舍弃那些虽有作用但重要性次之的部分。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah, it's a very sort of business school ex-consultant point of view that I do agree with and share, which is there's always three things or fewer, never more than three things. You have to have a nice round couple and if you have a fourth, you've got to figure out how to squish it in there because it just doesn't look right if there's four.
turns.zh: 是的，我完全认同这种商学院前顾问的观点：任何列表都应控制在三个或更少，绝不超过三个。要保持数字整齐，若有第四个要点，需想办法巧妙整合。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Agree. Yeah, even though I've been guilty of more than three, try hard to avoid it.
turns.zh: 同意。虽然我自己也曾犯过超过三个要点的错误，但现在努力避免了。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah, you're using notion and you have your three bullets expanding and there's sub bullets, but at least you have that top line.
turns.zh: 是的，你用的Notion平台，三个要点下有子项目，但至少结构清晰。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right. The other thing is I think that there's just a focus you need to get good at just like, people often want to lump together a bunch of ideas and then every time you do that it just dilutes everything. So, I think there's just a lot of power and pick the thing, pick the thing that's going to have the most impact and cut other stuff that may have some impact but is much less important.
turns.zh: 没错。还有一点，关键是要专注于最重要的内容。人们常想把一堆想法堆在一起，但这样只会冲淡整体效果。应该选取最具影响力的核心内容，舍弃那些虽有作用但重要性次之的部分。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: I think again, simplification is something and prioritization, which is sort of the same thing, gets tossed around a lot as a thing you have to get good at, but it's really challenging. Getting to the one thing you should do is extremely difficult and being able and having the gumption to say no to all those other things is really hard, because there's probably at any given time, 10 things you should do, but you can't do 10 things, you'll never be successful if you do that in a number of things. And so you have to pick one. (00:15:59): And so it's both figuring out how to get confident in your decision and then B, having the willingness, and maybe I should have added this to my what makes great PMs list, the willingness to make the bet and be responsible for it. And that's what I think separates the PM role from a lot of other roles and why it's such a challenging job when done right is because you have to be willing to take responsibility and it's your job to pick the thing and it's your job to be accountable to your team for picking the thing so you better get it right.
turns.zh: 我再想一想，简化和优先排序是同一个概念，但人们总把它们挂在嘴边，仿佛这是一项必须掌握的技能，但实际上这很难做到。确定你应该专注于哪件事极其困难，而能够拒绝其他所有事情的诱惑更是难上加难，因为任何时候可能都有10件你应该做的事，但你不可能同时做好10件事。如果你想在多项事情上出色，那注定会失败。所以你必须选定一件。（00:15:59）：这既需要学会如何对自己的决定充满信心，也需要具备勇气——或许我本该把这一点加到“优秀产品经理的特质”清单里——即敢于下注并为此负责的勇气。这就是产品经理角色与其他许多角色截然不同的地方，也是做好产品经理工作如此具有挑战性的原因——你必须愿意承担责任，选定重点任务，并对团队负责。因此，你必须选对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ownership such an important part of just being a PM. Again, coming back to this interview I just did with an ex Amazon guy, that's one of their principles at Amazon is just leaders, basically ownership, feeling like you have ownership of what you're working on.
turns.zh: “所有权”是产品经理角色的核心要素。再说回我刚完成的亚马逊前员工采访，亚马逊的核心原则之一就是领导者要具备所有权感，要觉得自己对正在做的工作拥有掌控权。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: I agree, but to me at least the word ownership doesn't have the same oh shit feeling as you're making a bet. You make a bet, that means you know that there's a chance that the thing you're working on is not going to work out and you still have to be the one to do the thing, jump off the ledge, drop in on the ski run. So, ownership to me never signaled that risk that I think comes with being a PM.
turns.zh: 我同意，但至少对我来说，“所有权”这个词没有那种“天啊，我在下注”的紧迫感。下注意味着你知道自己所做之事可能失败，但你仍必须承担责任，必须勇往直前、迎难而上。所以，对我来说，“所有权”从未传递出我认为产品经理角色所附带的风险感。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Good point. On the simplify concept, it reminds me at Airbnb, one of the core values at Airbnb for time was simplify. Is this idea that we should always try to be simplifying, and then it turned out the founders realized we're not actually great at this and it's unfair for us to say this is a value for not doing it. So, they actually cut it as a core value because their feeling was we shouldn't have aspirational values, we should reflect who we actually are, and they actually cut two different values to be more clear, even though they still want to simplify, they're just like, we're not actually good at this, so why are we pretending like we are.
turns.zh: 说得好。关于简化这个概念，这让我想起Airbnb。他们最初的核心价值观之一就是“简化”。但后来创始人意识到，他们自己并不擅长做到这一点，所以不能把“简化”作为价值观却又要求别人去践行。于是他们干脆将其从核心价值观中删除，因为他们觉得不应该设定不切实际的愿景，而是要忠实于自身实际。尽管他们仍然想简化，但他们坦言自己做不到，所以何必假装能做到呢？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: I think maybe I'm good at it on paper, but there's been many times where I've been in situations where things are not simple and you just have to keep fighting for it.
turns.zh: 我觉得自己可能只是理论上擅长，但实际遇到复杂情况时，还是得不断为之奋斗。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Someone's trying to think about, okay, I want to become better as a PM and I'm going to try to start simplifying. What are examples of simplifying? Is it reduce your email length? Is it one pager focus? What are these buckets of things? And then also if there's an example of something you've simplified that comes to mind
turns.zh: 有人可能会想，嗯，我想成为更优秀的产品经理，所以要开始简化。简化的例子有哪些呢？是缩短邮件长度？还是用一页纸的重点汇报？这些都是哪些范畴？如果大家能想到自己简化过的例子，那就更好了。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: On what to simplify and more specifics, I would say anything can be simplified and shortened. Maybe another way to say shorten it. Definitely emails. I read them sometimes don't love them. Make them short. The Minto principle is something that I would recommend everyone do, which is put the headline, the full conclusion first and then you're supporting argument second.
turns.zh: 关于简化和具体内容，我想说任何东西都可以简化和缩短。或许还有其他简化它的方法。比如邮件，我有时会读邮件，但不太喜欢它们。一定要让邮件简短。明托原则是我推荐大家都应该遵循的，即先放置标题和最终结论，再逐步展开论点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have a newsletter post about that exact concept that people that I will link in the show notes that gives you-
turns.zh: 我有一篇关于这个概念的时事通讯文章，我会在节目笔记中附上链接——

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Fantastic.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The Minto Pyramid principle.
turns.zh: 明托金字塔原则。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yes, everyone should do that. A lot of new PMs fall into the trap of thinking that they should have some sort of buildup. Don't do that. Just tell me whatever the thing is, everyone will thank you. Doing things like that, things like you said, limiting your strategy docs, your conclusions, your next steps to three things maximum. I would generally say a rule of thumb would be pretty much every doc you write, you can delete the first two paragraphs that you've written. You don't need them. My dad, again, to go back to my dad when I would write, and this sounds cruel, but I promise it wasn't. When I would write a paper for school, he would just, and this is we didn't really have computers, whatever, he would just take away the first page and he'd be like, just start here. He would go, "Everything on the first page is crapola, don't use it." (00:19:30): And he wouldn't even read it, which would drive me crazy. He would just like, "Oh, it's crap. I don't care about that." So, I would do that and then just get other people, there's probably somebody around you that's good and find people to edit your work and to look at it. I have a little Slack workspace that has three people in it, me and two other women who are product leaders, and we oftentimes send each other our work still and we say, "Hey, I'm struggling with this. Can you read it? Help me make it simpler. Can you help me fix this up?" And we do that for each other. So, find a peer maybe who's in a non-competitive space who can do that for you. I mean I still use those people to help me.
turns.zh: 是的，每个人都应该这么做。很多新晋产品经理会陷入一个误区，认为自己需要铺垫一些背景内容。别这样做。直接告诉大家重点就行，每个人都会感激你的。比如你提到的那些做法，比如把策略文档、结论和下一步行动限制在最多三点之内。我通常的经验法则是，几乎每份你写的文档都可以删掉前两段。它们没用。我父亲，回到我小时候写论文的经历，这听起来可能有点严厉，但我保证他不是故意的。当我为学校写论文时，他会直接拿走第一页，然后说："就从这里开始吧。"他会说："第一页的都是垃圾，别用了。"（00:19:30）他甚至都不读内容，这让我很抓狂。他只是说："哦，太烂了。我才不在乎呢。"所以我会这么做，然后找其他人帮忙。身边可能有做产品经理的优秀人士，可以让他们帮你审稿和润色。我有一个Slack工作区，里面有三个人，包括我和另外两位产品负责人，我们经常互相发送工作成果，互相说："嘿，我写这个遇到了难题。你能看看吗？帮我简化一下？"我们互相帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is extremely cool. Can you talk more about this group that you have?
turns.zh: 这太棒了。能多聊聊你这个小组吗？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah, I don't know if it's a group. It's like three friends. Shout out Alexa and Daphne. Yeah, I mean the three of us all worked together when we were at Drift. We've stayed in touch and I've just found that in order to be good at your job continuously, you need people who can help give you feedback, and the more senior you get, the harder that is. And so having people who can give you another point of view who maybe you can vent to if it's not appropriate as a leader who can give you other experiences that they're going through has been incredibly valuable. And so we just have a little group chat that is focused on product.
turns.zh: 是的，我不知道这算不算一个小组。就是三个朋友。向Alexa和Daphne致敬。是的，我们在Drift工作时就一起共事过。一直保持联系。我发现，要持续做好本职工作，需要有人给你反馈。职位越高，越难做到这一点。所以有能给你另一种视角的人——如果你作为领导不方便倾诉——能给你分享经验的人，这太有价值了。所以我们就组建了一个专注于产品的小组聊天室。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so cool. Is there a tip you could share for someone that wants to create something like this? Is it important for you to have worked with them before? Is Slack a good way to communicate? Anything there that's just like, oh yeah, here's a cool tip.
turns.zh: 太棒了。对于想创建这样小组的人，有什么建议吗？必须和他们合作过才行吗？Slack是沟通的好方式吗？有没有什么特别的技巧可以分享？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Slack just worked for us where we are during the day, and I think having easy access to it was important. You could probably use WhatsApp or a literal group text. There are small community, there's one, I worked in healthcare for a year and a bit, and there's a Slack community that somebody organized for heads of products and healthcare startups that is similar to those really, really powerful and a really great space to be in. And so you just have to kind of suss out where these things are. You work with amazing people and there's people around you who are going to become your friends, and so keep an eye out for them and keep in touch with them when you leave a job because you never know when they might become your little Slack workspace.
turns.zh: 斯莱克（Slack）在我们日常工作中非常顺手，随时能访问它很重要。你或许也可以用WhatsApp或者群发短信。不过有些社区规模较小，比如我曾在医疗保健领域工作过一年多，有人为产品负责人和医疗保健初创公司组建了一个Slack社区，效果非常好。所以你只需要去挖掘这些资源。与优秀的人共事，他们可能会成为你的朋友，离职后也要保持联系，因为说不定哪天他们就会成为你Slack工作区的核心成员。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, I love it. Okay, I'm glad we talked on that. Okay, back on track. The second bucket you described as following up on results, is it just do that. Is there anything more you can add there?
turns.zh: 哦，我太喜欢这个观点了。好的，很高兴我们能聊到这点。回到正题。你提到第二个要点是跟进结果，那具体该怎么做呢？有没有什么额外建议？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: I put reminders in my calendar. I mean, yeah, it's just do that. But if you're launching a product, usually you release something and you have that initial push of a couple of weeks where you're finding bugs and you're maybe you're pulling metrics and everyone remembers it, then I would remember two weeks after that, a month after that, six months after that, put a reminder in your calendar to check your dashboard or check the metrics or check whatever it is that you were doing, and you won't forget and then share them with whoever might care about it. And it's as simple as that.
turns.zh: 我会在日历里设置提醒。没错，就是这么简单。但如果你要推出新产品，通常刚发布时会有几周的推广期，期间会发现漏洞、收集数据，大家都很关注。但两周后、一个月后、半年后，你需要在日历里设置提醒，检查仪表板、数据指标或者其他关键项，这样就不会遗漏了。然后把这些信息分享给可能感兴趣的人，就这么简单。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is the reason this is one of the three things you think are most consistent across great PMs, that it helps your manager see you like, wow, Maggie's so on top of everything, or is it more that you learn from that experience and drive more impact or is it both?
turns.zh: 为什么你认为这是优秀产品经理最一致的三个特质之一？是因为这能让经理对你刮目相看——哇，Maggie真是掌控全局，还是因为你从中吸取经验、创造更大影响力，或者两者兼而有之？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: It's definitely both. I'm not going to pretend like if you're just great at your job quietly that you're going to get what you want. Just if you're toiling in the background, doing a great job getting results. If you have a great manager, maybe you'll be successful. Great managers are few and far between, and I am of the opinion that I never wanted to rely on someone else to get what I wanted. And so I would always make sure to share that, always make sure to share my progress because I didn't want to leave it up to chance that someone would notice. So, I would suggest doing it for both reasons. And that's one of those things that people want to pretend that everything's perfect and we're all great and we're always going to get what we want and always going to get that promotion, but you have to work for it.
turns.zh: 两者皆有。我不会假装只要默默做好工作就能如愿以偿。光是埋头苦干、取得成果固然重要，但如果有优秀的经理，可能更容易成功。优秀的经理实属难得，而我从不指望靠别人来实现目标。所以我会确保分享进展，避免让别人忽视你的努力。我建议两者兼顾。这正是人们总想假装一切完美、自己无所不能、总能升职的缘故，但成功需要靠自己努力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that point. It reminds me what I find one of the most important traits of a great product manager is they create this aura that they've got this, they put something on their plate and they're not going to drop it, that the threads are not going to be forgotten. And this connects to me there. They feel like Maggie's going to tell me what happened with this experiment. I don't have to think about it as a manager.
turns.zh: 我很认同这一点。它让我想起优秀产品经理最重要的特质之一：他们营造出一种掌控全局的氛围，一旦接手某项任务绝不放手，不让任何线索被遗忘。这点我深有共鸣。比如我总觉得Maggie会跟我汇报实验结果，作为经理我根本不用操心这些。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah, that's a really good point. And then you mentioned this a little bit ago, the side benefit is that you learn more. You will go back and learn why something happened or why it didn't happen, and the more that you follow up on what you've been doing and the more you learn, the better you get every time you ship something. To me, the other answer of what makes a great PM is family shipped a lot of stuff. The more you ship, the more you learn. And that's why it can take years to build up expertise because you just have to ship a lot of stuff.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实是个很棒的观点。你之前也提到过，这还有一个额外的好处——你能学到更多东西。当你回顾过去，思考某件事为何发生或未能发生时，当你不断追踪自己的工作进展并不断学习时，每次发布新成果时你都会变得更出色。在我看来，成为一名优秀产品经理的另一个关键因素是多参与项目。越是频繁地发布产品，你就能学到越多东西。这也是为什么积累专业技能需要多年时间，因为你必须不断实践。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a lot of people that are always frustrated. They're not getting promoted quickly enough as a PM. They're not moving off the ladder like, oh my god, I've been a PM for two years. I'm not a senior PM yet. Can you speak more to just that thought and just how long it takes to get actually good? I guess I'll share briefly in my experience, it took me four years to actually know what the hell I was doing as a PM and then things started to really take off. What's your experience?
turns.zh: 很多人总是感到沮丧。他们晋升产品经理的速度不够快。他们的职业阶梯似乎停滞不前——比如，天啊，我做产品经理两年了，还是不是高级产品经理。你能否详细谈谈这个问题，以及真正精通这份工作需要多长时间？我简单分享一下自己的经历：我花了四年时间才真正明白自己在做什么，之后才开始取得真正的进展。你有什么经验吗？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: I would say similarly, it took a lot of years to feel confident that I knew what I was doing. My first PM job was a product management rotation job at TripAdvisor. I had no PM background. It was after business school and I left those two years thinking, yeah, I've worked on four different teams over the two years. I've shipped all this stuff, I'm good. Went to a startup, there was another product person there, they left and I was the only product person at the startup. And I realized really quickly, I had no idea what I was doing. I had no one to learn from. I had only had two years of experience and I was not ready for that job. I didn't feel confident in the decisions I was making. That's why I joined Drift is because that team had all these really incredible product thinkers on it and they were shipping all sorts of stuff. They had all this momentum and I thought, okay, that's where I'm going to go to learn. (00:25:29): And so then two more years. So, that's five years until I really felt like I knew what I was doing. And that's because it takes a long time to ship stuff. And so to people who want to progress, you can progress by job hopping, you can progress by going in and out of startups. But to me staying at that, when I was at Drip, I was there for almost four years. I got to see two or three cycles of the same product and I learned more from that than I did out of the year or so I spent doing other things each at a time because you got to see the consequences of your decisions and that's rare. And people, myself included, of course you want to get promoted, of course you want to move up. I'm ambitious. Lots of people are ambitious, but for better or for worse, spending the time is really helpful and I think allowed me to move faster later because I had just spent the time grinding it out for a while in order to be better later.
turns.zh: 我也有类似的经历。花了很多年才有信心认为自己做得不错。我第一份产品经理工作是在TripAdvisor的轮岗项目中完成的。我没有产品经理背景，那是在商学院毕业后做的。那两年结束时，我离开公司时觉得，自己在四个不同团队工作过，发布了不少产品，应该还不错。后来去了一家初创公司，那里只有我一个产品经理。很快我就意识到，自己完全不知道在做什么。没有可以学习的对象，仅有的两年经验根本不足以胜任那份工作。我对自己的决策缺乏信心。这就是我加入Drift的原因——那支团队里有许多极具产品思维的人，他们不断发布新成果，充满活力。我当时就想，嗯，我要去那里学习。（00:25:29）又过了两年。总之，花了五年时间我才真正觉得自己掌握了诀窍。这是因为发布新成果需要大量时间。因此，想要晋升的人可以通过跳槽或频繁加入初创公司来实现。但对我来说，在Drift待了近四年更有意义。我见证了同一款产品的两三个迭代周期，从中学到的东西远超在其他公司短暂工作的效果，因为你能看到自己决策的后果，而这在其他地方是很难获得的。当然，人人都想晋升，都想往上爬，我也雄心勃勃。很多人也是如此，但无论好坏，多花时间磨砺自己确实很有帮助，我相信这让我日后能更快地进步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, is that advice you often give of go deep into a company or a product versus just bounce and track a bunch of different companies or depends?
turns.zh: 那么，你常给出的建议是深入一家公司或一个产品，还是频繁跳槽、追踪不同公司的情况？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: It depends. There are lots of really good reasons to bounce. I've done it, many people have done it, but I was surprised at how much I value that experience of having stuck around for a while and how much I learned from it was something I hadn't expected going into it, especially because you don't hear that point of view as much or as I wasn't hearing that point of view as much when I was thinking about the sort of arc of my career, but I'm glad that I did it. And then of course people always want to get promoted, always ask that question and my answer is always create impact and that can take time.
turns.zh: 这得看情况。有很多充分的理由去尝试跳槽。我自己就经历过多次跳槽，很多人也都这么做过，但让我惊讶的是，我越发珍视那种坚持下去的经历，以及从中获得的成长——这远超我最初的预期。尤其是在规划职业生涯时，我并未过多考虑这种长期投入的重要性，但现在看来，这段经历确实意义非凡。我很庆幸自己当时的选择。当然，人们总想升职，总会问这个问题，而我的回答始终是：创造价值，而这可能需要时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: At my first job, I was there for nine years and then I started a company for a year and a half and then we sold to Airbnb, and then I was at Airbnb for seven years. So, I'm very much on that train of just, not that I intended for that to happen, but I definitely went deep and I think there's pros and cons, but there's so many pros to that, so many reasons. Okay. Let's talk about the last part, which is the third point you made, which is carrying the water, I think is how you described it.
turns.zh: 在我的第一份工作中，我待了九年。之后，我创办了一家公司，一年半后将其出售给Airbnb，随后在Airbnb工作了七年。所以，我的人生轨迹就是这样——并非刻意为之，但确实深耕其中。我认为这有利有弊，但利远大于弊。好的，让我们来谈谈最后一点，即你提到的第三个观点——"默默付出"，我记得你就是这么形容的。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah. This one, there's no tips and tricks. It's just do the work. If you ever find yourself saying something like, that's not my job, that's probably a thing you should do. And you know what? It probably isn't your job and it probably is someone else's job and you can spend your life getting frustrated at that or you can just get over and get the work done. And people who are willing to just get the work done will move faster, their products will be more successful and they probably aren't carrying around all that anger and crappy emotion. (00:28:17): Because we touched on this earlier as a PM for better or for worse, and maybe this is not how we all want it to be, but you're oftentimes the emotional center of the team and it's your job to keep people motivated, keep people excited, keep them bought into the project, and you just have to keep that optimism going. And it's hard work. It's really hard work to stay positive and to keep people amped for that thing. And part of it can be just like, you know what? Let me take that on. Let me grab that, whatever. I'll do this thing. I'll hop on this sales call, I'll implement this with the customer. You just have to do whatever it takes.
turns.zh: 是的。对于这一点，并没有什么技巧或捷径。只需埋头苦干即可。如果你发现自己在说"这不是我的工作"，那很可能就是你该做的事。说实话，这或许确实不是你的工作，很可能是别人的职责。你可以终日为此感到沮丧，也可以在完成任务后释然。那些甘愿埋头工作的人会进展得更快，他们的产品也会更成功，而且他们可能不会被各种负面情绪所困扰。（00:28:17）：因为我们之前在谈及产品经理时曾提到，无论好坏，你往往是团队的情感核心，你的职责是保持团队的积极性，激发他们的热情，让他们全心投入项目。你必须始终保持这种乐观态度。要保持积极向上，并让大家为项目充满热情，这实在不易。有时你只需说一句："好吧，让我来接手吧。"或者"我来处理这个问题吧。"你必须全力以赴。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me of one of your lessons that you shared, in one of your podcast episodes. It was one of your PM lessons of 2021, and the lesson was, when in doubt it's your job as a PM, which I think relates very much to which it just shared. Can you speak to that?
turns.zh: 这让我想起你曾在播客中分享的一个经验教训。那是2021年你分享的产品经理经验之一，核心观点是：当你心存疑虑时，作为产品经理，你的职责就是勇往直前。我觉得这与你刚刚分享的内容高度契合。你能谈谈这一点吗？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: It might actually make sense to put this in the context of the other roles that are part of the team. So, as an engineer, your job is to write the code to really reduce this down and build the thing and make it work to spec. As a designer, maybe your job is to design the thing, design the solution, design the user experience. Obviously there's lots more complexity in that role. Design your amazing engineering, your amazing TLDR, caveat, whatever. But as a PM, you don't have that thing, right? (00:29:41): It's not like, oh, my job is just to write the one-pager. That's not true. Your job isn't just to pick the problem. Your job is to deliver a business result. And so you're uniquely positioned to have to fill in all the gaps because no one else is incentivized to do that. As an engineer, you can finish your work and hand it off and say, I did it, and the good ones care, but you don't have to care. As a PM, you're not going to do your job unless that problem gets solved for the customer or the user at the end of the day. And so your job is to make sure everything happens for that product.
turns.zh: 或许将这件事置于团队中其他角色的背景下会更合理。作为工程师，你的职责是编写代码以简化整个流程，构建产品并确保其符合规格。作为设计师，你的任务可能是设计产品、规划解决方案、优化用户体验。显然，设计师的职责更为复杂——设计出惊艳的工程方案，撰写简洁明了的摘要，附加免责声明等等。但作为产品经理，你却没有这些优势，对吧？（00:29:41）这可不是说"我的工作就是写一份简介"。事实并非如此。你的职责不只是选定问题，而是要交付商业成果。因此，你需要填补所有空白，因为其他人没有这样的动力去做到这一点。工程师完成工作后可以移交任务并说"我完成了"，优秀的工程师会关注质量，但你不必为此负责。而产品经理只有在最终为客户或用户解决问题时才能算完成任务。因此，你的职责是确保产品开发的每个环节都顺利推进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me of another interview you did where you talked about how a lot of the PM job sucks. It's not as glamorous as people often think, and most of the job is these really boring, annoying things. I guess, is there anything you want to add there of just a lot of people want to get into PM, they're like, oh, I'm going to run the show. It's going to be so great. I'm going to be a product manager and tell people what to do. But that's not how it is.
turns.zh: 这让我想起你之前的一次采访，你提到产品经理的工作其实很糟糕。它并不像人们想象的那样光鲜亮丽，大部分工作都是些无聊又烦人的事情。我猜，有很多人想进入产品经理领域，他们会想，"哦，我要掌控全局。肯定很棒。我要成为产品经理，告诉别人该做什么。"但现实并非如此。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: It's just one of those things that people, and when I joined product, it was just sort of becoming a cool job. It wasn't the hot job on campus when I was in business school. That was more private equity, venture capital. And now there's a sense of cachet around it. But again, it comes back to that earlier point, which is you do get to do cool stuff. You get to decide what gets built. That's cool. You have a lot of ownership like we talked about. You could see it as you have a lot of power, but at the same time you're responsible. (00:31:12): And so with that comes this responsibility to get it right, to make the right bets, ship the right products, get them out the door. And so there's a lot of bullshit work you have to do. Again, project management is one everyone hates on. QA is a really good one. You should QA your products. That's great if you have a QA team, you should QA them. You should know how they work. You should implement with your customers, you should be able to sell them, you should be able to find users. All that stuff is stuff that you should be able to do, and none of it is above you.
turns.zh: 这只是人们常犯的误区。我加入产品团队时，它刚开始被视为一份很酷的工作。当我在商学院时，私募股权和风险投资可比产品经理更受追捧。如今，产品经理又有了某种光环。但归根结底，还是要回到之前的观点——你确实能做很酷的事情。你可以决定建造什么产品。这很棒。你能感受到自主权，正如我们所讨论的。你可以把这视为拥有巨大权力，但与此同时你也要承担责任。（00:31:12）因此，伴随而来的是确保决策正确、押注准确、推出正确的产品并将其推向市场的责任。你必须做很多琐碎的工作。再说项目管理，人人都讨厌它。QA也是个很好的例子。你应该对产品进行QA测试。如果有QA团队，你应该亲自测试。了解他们的工作原理。与客户一起实施产品，学会销售产品，寻找用户。所有这些都是你应该具备的能力，没有任何工作是高高在上的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If someone is listening and they're not a PM and they are not convinced to not get into product manager, they still want to become a PM, what is your best advice for selling that is trying to get into product management of how to actually break into product management?
turns.zh: 如果有听众不是产品经理，但仍不死心想进入产品经理领域，想成为产品经理，你能给出什么最佳建议来说服他们进入产品管理呢？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: I thought about this one a lot and I consulted the Slack workspace team. Because it's been a long time since I've tried to get into product. And so I didn't know what was going on these days because it's hard and I don't know if things have changed. I went to business school and that's how I got in. There was a program that took MBA students. I think there are some entry-level programs out there, big tech companies, if you can get them, I think they're really hard to get because they're very few and far between. And so the most common two paths that I've seen are people who switched laterally within a company. Again, challenging but can be done. Or people who joined startups. So, when I was at my last startup, I did hire someone who was coming out of business school who hadn't been into product into a PM role. And I can't say I wouldn't do it because it was awesome and she was amazing, but it takes a lot of work. (00:32:49): The reason why people don't do it is because as a manager, it takes a lot of work because there's so much that these people need to learn. And what we ended up doing is she and I spent four months working together in a WeWork in person to help her onboard really quickly into the role, which was so rewarding. And I loved every second of it, and I wish I could do that again and again and again. But to get that, she basically just hounded me. Christina, if you're listening, you emailed me a lot. We talked a lot and we waited until the time was right and then you finally convinced me to do it. So, I don't know. I don't if there's a reliable path that I can say this is what my advice would be other than try a startup network. See what you can do.
turns.zh: 我对此思考了很多，还咨询了Slack工作区团队。因为我已经很久没尝试进入产品领域了。所以我不了解如今的行业动态，毕竟这条路很艰难，而且我也不确定情况是否有所变化。我曾就读于商学院，通过这个途径进入了产品领域。当时有一个项目，专门招收MBA学生。我觉得现在也有一些入门级项目，大型科技公司也会有这类机会，但这些机会非常难得，僧多粥少。常见的两条路径是：一是横向调动到同一家公司；二是加入初创公司。我在上一家初创公司时，就曾聘请过一位刚从商学院毕业、毫无产品经验的人担任PM职位。我不能说我不推荐这种做法——她非常出色，但这确实需要付出巨大努力。（00:32:49）人们不愿意这么做的原因在于，作为管理者，需要投入大量精力去帮助新人快速上手。我们最终的解决方案是，她和我在WeWork办公室共事了四个月，帮助她快速适应角色，这个过程收获满满。我至今仍热爱那段时光，真希望能重来无数次。但要做到这一点，她简直把我缠得不行。克里斯蒂娜，如果你正在听的话，你当时给我发了很多邮件。我们聊了很多，等待时机成熟，最终你成功说服了我。所以，我也不确定是否有可靠的路径可以给出建议，除了尝试加入初创公司网络，看看能做些什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you've made up this point elsewhere, which I think is an additional key piece is once you have a PM title on your resume, everything gets easier. As a hiring manager, I'm just like, I look at a resume like, oh, they've never been a PM. This isn't the role. It's rarely that someone wants someone that's never been a PM.
turns.zh: 你之前在其他地方也提到过一个关键点：一旦简历上有了PM头衔，一切都会变得容易得多。作为招聘经理，我看到简历时会想，哦，他们从未担任过PM。这不是合适的角色。很少有人会想要没有PM经验的人。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah. And I tell people, I do unsurprisingly talk to lots of people who either are in product or want to be in product. And that's one of the things I always tell them because if they're deciding between roles and they have an opportunity to do something, and my advice is always, if you can get someone to stamp you with the product manager role, take it. Because to your point, it's what we screen on. It's for better or for worse, it's just like you have to get that first job. And then once you get that first job, it all gets easier. You can get in and then you can talk about your experience because then the second question I have is, what have you shipped? So, it's like, have you been at PM before? What have you shipped? And it's fascinating how quickly people can't answer that question. And the people who can are always several steps ahead of the people.
turns.zh: 是的。我经常告诉人们（不出所料，我和很多从事或想从事产品工作的人交流过），我会反复强调这一点：如果你正在权衡不同职位机会，遇到有机会担任PM的职位，就一定要抓住它。因为正如你所说，我们筛选候选人时会看重这一点。无论好坏，关键在于你必须获得第一份PM工作。一旦获得这份工作，一切都会变得容易许多。你可以进入这个领域，然后谈论你的经验，因为接下来我会问：你之前做过产品吗？你交付过什么成果？令人惊讶的是，很多人根本答不上来这个问题。能回答的人总是比其他人领先好几步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's shift topics and talk about product strategy. Many people are told you need to get better product strategy. You're not great at strategy. A lot of people are also just confused, what is strategy? How do I get better at strategy? How do we describe a strategy? And you have a really great explanation and overview of how to think about this stuff. So, I'd love to hear your take on just how do you actually write out and describe a strategy.
turns.zh: 让我们转换话题，聊聊产品策略。很多人被告知需要提升产品策略能力，但他们对策略不擅长。许多人也感到困惑：什么是策略？如何提升策略能力？如何描述一份策略？你对此有非常精彩的解释和概述。所以，我很想听听你对如何实际撰写和描述策略的看法。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Sure, yeah. And another thing that happens, and I'll give the outline, but another thing I hear, especially as you get further in your career, and unfortunately if you're maybe an underrepresented person in tech, is that you need to be more strategic. And so that's feedback that almost always happens, especially if you're a woman in product, in tech who's knocking at the door of a leadership role. You've probably gotten that feedback. And so I made it my mission to figure out what the heck is this thing? How do I do it? How can I do it in a way that is demonstrable so that I'm never getting that feedback that's like, oh, she's not strategic. And so what I did was something that I kind of did in the background because I had an engineer who I worked with who really wanted to understand why we were doing what we were doing, and he was not satisfied with sort of a surface level answer. (00:35:57): And he was just pushing and pushing and pushing. And so what I did was I just wrote out a Google doc and I started with like, okay, and not fancy, these are just bullets. What is the mission? What is the point of the company? What are our goals? Maybe we have some sort of high level framing of what we're working on. And then I had this big section that was just the landscape. And in that section I put in what's going on with our business? What's happening with our products? What's our point of view on the market? Who are our competitors? A SWOT analysis, key risks that we might be facing. Just dump that all on paper. Then what are the current quarters business goals or however you do planning, what are the current things that your company's working on? Then I put in, all right, that's sort of the context that we're operating in. (00:36:44): Then I wanted to understand where are we. So what is an honest accounting of the current state of your product, the business overall, and then the specific area that you're working in. What works, what doesn't work? What are your customers saying? Bottoms up feedback, users, customers, teams, what are your support tickets? Get that all out on paper. And then really importantly, where are your technical hurdles? What are the big pieces of tech debt? What are your engineering and technical teams always harping on that they want to invest in? Are there some big things coming down the pipe that you need to think about? Just get everything on paper. And then usually in the process of writing all that down, you'll start to see, okay, I kind of get where we are. I kind of get what the challenge is. And then you write a section that's like, what's the opportunity? (00:37:34): From all of that, what's going to bubble up as the top one or two opportunities for your team? Where do you want to play? Where can you win? Where's the unique? Based on your unique competitive advantage, where do you think you all should be and why? And then based on that opportunity, what are the challenges? So, what's going to be the hardest about taking advantage of that? What has to be, another way to frame it is what has to be true about the world for that to work? That's a one that's been helpful. And then what would you do? Take a swing at writing down your solution, what you would need to build, how might it work? Anything that you have, this is where I would say three bullets, maybe what you might want to do and then a plan. If no one else had an opinion, how would you go about it? (00:38:26): How would you sequence it? What would you do? How might you get the team to work on it? What would your team have to look like? How much would it cost to do it? All that you can start to layer in all that kind of stuff. And then I just share the doc. Share it with everybody. There should not be any secret. And you should be able to walk all the way from your company's mission down to the individual priority on your team and see the logic chain and why you got there. And if anyone doesn't agree with it, they can call out where their disagreement lands in that landscape. But at least then you've put everything on paper, you understand how you got to where you're going, and then you can have an argument about the different pieces and points of data and feedback that you're getting, but at least people understand how you got where you got. And then it doesn't become like, I don't agree with you. It becomes, I don't agree with this point.
turns.zh:
好的，没问题。还有另外一件事，我经常遇到的，尤其是在职业生涯中晋升阶段，如果你恰好是科技行业中被边缘化的人群，就会被告知需要更具战略眼光。这类反馈我听得太多了。比如，如果你是一位在产品或技术领域敲开领导岗位大门的女性，可能就会听到类似"你不够有战略思维"的批评。于是我决心探究其背后的深层原因：如何才能真正做到战略清晰？

（00:35:57）我当时找了一位工程师同事，他总想了解我们工作的意义，普通的解释根本无法满足他。于是我写了一份Google文档，内容分为几个部分：首先是使命陈述，公司的核心目标；其次是宏观环境分析，包括市场动态、竞争对手、SWOT分析等；然后是当前业务目标和工程团队的优先事项；最后是技术挑战和机遇。

（00:36:44）接下来，我需要审视现状：产品现状、市场反馈、用户痛点、技术债务等问题。通过梳理这些信息，我逐渐明确了团队的核心挑战和机遇，进而制定行动计划。

（00:37:34）最后，要确定团队的核心机遇：基于独特竞争优势，如何突破技术瓶颈，抓住市场机遇。然后，针对每个机遇，拆解关键挑战，确保团队能够高效执行。
做这件事需要花多少钱？你可以逐步整合所有相关内容。然后我只需把文档分享给所有人。不应该有任何秘密。你们应该能够从公司的使命一路追溯到团队的个体优先事项，理解其中的逻辑链条，以及为何会得出这样的结论。如果有人对此有异议，他们可以指出异议所在。但至少这样一来，你把所有内容都落实到纸面上，清楚自己是如何达成目标的。之后，你们可以就不同的观点、数据和反馈展开讨论，但至少大家都能理解最终决策的依据。这样争论就不会演变成“我不同意你的观点”，而是变成“我不同意这个具体论点”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is such a cool way of doing it. By the way, is there a template that we can point people to that has this sort of-

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: There's not, I've only ever done it in a loose Google doc and then it just grows and changes. I can maybe try to write up those bullets, but it's just like I just make headers and then I just start dumping content in it.
turns.zh: 没有，我以前都是在一个松散的Google文档里做的，然后它就不断扩充和变化。我或许可以试着把那些要点写出来，但我就是先做个标题，然后再往里填内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 是啊，这正是人们需要的。如果你在这一期播客发布前能完成这个模板，我们会把它放进节目笔记里。如果不行的话，人们可以直接在Twitter上找你或者问Maggie，我们提到的那个模板在哪里？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah, I'm happy to write it on a piece of paper and take a photo of it and send it around.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There you go. Just make it really grainy and an artifact. We found Maggie's template. This is awesome. So, I've never heard of a version of this with so much depth into the landscape, and I think that's so smart because so much of conflict and disagreement comes from you just don't have the same information or the manager, exec or whatever doesn't think you have the information. So, if you just lean into, here's everything that I know and here's what's happening, and if you disagree with this goal, tell me, and then it'll change the plan.
turns.zh: 好的，就把它拍得模糊一点，让它看起来是手写的。我们找到了Maggie的模板。这太棒了。所以，我从未听说过有这么深入洞察行业全貌的版本，我觉得这太明智了，因为很多冲突和分歧都源于你没有相同的信息，或者经理、执行团队之类的认为你没有这些信息。所以，如果你就坚持说，我知道的这些情况就是这样，正在发生这些事，如果你对这个目标有异议，请告诉我，然后我们再调整计划。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Part of it's also that typically speaking, when you're doing a strategy, you're doing it at a higher level. So, I don't think every product needs a strategy. Every feature doesn't need a strategy for example, you don't need to do this if you're working on a tiny slice of a product and you have user feedback, don't overcomplicate it, just do the stuff that makes sense. But especially as I've gotten more senior in my career, the questions are bigger and the impact is broader and the timelines are longer. And honestly, it was also because I wanted to get it right. I didn't want to make a bet on something and put a bunch of resources against a problem and get it wrong. And so this was also homework that I wanted to do for myself to know that I was going to do the right thing. For some reason, I'm always paranoid that other people have more information or doing it better than I'm doing it. (00:41:11): So, I was like, okay, I have to write it all down and then make sure I got it right and share it with everyone and make sure that they agreed with me so that I didn't screw this thing up. And it just was such a useful exercise that I kept doing it. And of course people don't read it. People only read a tiny section. You'll run into the same problems you run in with everything else, but at least I knew that I had done the work and if people cared to engage with it was there.
turns.zh: 部分原因还在于，通常来说，当你制定战略时，都是在更高的层面做的。所以，我不认为每个产品都需要战略。例如，每个功能都不需要战略，如果你只负责产品的一个小模块，并且有用户反馈，就不必把事情复杂化，只要做些有意义的事就行。但随着我在职业生涯中晋升得越高，面临的问题就越大，影响也越广，时间线也越长。说实话，也是因为我想把事情做对。我不想在某个问题上押注，然后投入大量资源却做错了。所以这也是我为自己做的“功课”，确保我能做出正确的决策。出于某种原因，我总是担心别人有更多信息或者做得比我好得多。（00:41:11）所以我就会想，好吧，我必须把所有内容都写下来，然后确保准确无误，分享给所有人，确保他们也认同我的观点，这样我就不会把事情搞砸了。而这恰恰是一个非常有用的练习，所以我一直坚持做下去。当然，人们并不读它。他们只会看一小部分。你会遇到和其他事情一样的问题，但至少我知道我已经完成了这项工作，如果人们愿意参与其中，那资料就在那里。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley

You can kind of get the point and the suggestion on what I think we should do or what the strategy should be, should be customizable in that section. turns.zh: 至于实际内容，最后我会写一个总结，回归到明特奥原则（Minto principle）。整个过程我会先完成所有内容，然后把总结放在顶部，这样用户就能在首页上方一目了然。如果你愿意，可以把它称作“首屏内容”。你能通过这个部分大致理解我的观点和建议，了解我们应该采取的策略或流程。当然，策略部分可以根据需求进行调整。但有时内容会长达20页——比如当你需要深入分析竞争对手，或是关注有趣的市场动态和技术变革时。有些时候我会截取其他公司的营销网站截图并放入文档中，其中可能包含一些有价值的见解。所以，文档不必只有文字，可以包含各种你想添加的元素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you made the point that it's not like you expect people to read this whole thing. turns.zh: 你提到用户不必通读整个文档。这里有个总结部分能让他们快速获取结论。理论上，如果他们想深入研究，还能继续阅读。但关键在于如何平衡两者——既要写得全面，又不能太冗长，让人望而却步。最终目标是提供实用内容，并附上总结。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: It comes back to the reason why I write the document in the first place. And that's for me. So, it's my homework to do my job effectively. I just make sure to share it. turns.zh: 这让我回想起最初写这份文档的初衷。其实这是为自己服务的——确保自己能高效完成工作。关键是分享成果。我发现，尤其是工程和设计团队，如果是真正的三角合作模式，他们往往会深入研究文档，因为他们也身处一线，需要确保团队成员能真正认同你的项目理念。（00:43:28）有时候团队中的初级成员也会参与其中，他们会很感兴趣，甚至深入探讨。当然，也会有人只浏览前几页，要么说"不错"，要么"你太蠢了，我讨厌这个"。这种情况总是存在的。所以我从不强求所有人通读全文。关键是我需要通过这份文档增强自己的决策信心，然后推动讨论，所以结果比过程更重要。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah, there are many, many times when if you combine this artifact and process with the point about simplification where through that process you just start cutting so many things because then what happens is, let's say you've gone through this exercise and you're like, okay, I know exactly what my three things are that I want to work on. Then there's a moment where you take the strategy and then you look at your roadmap and they're never the same. And the roadmap is just bloated with all of this random stuff that like, oh, well, we have to do that because of this, or we have to do that because of that. (00:47:37): This thing we're still working on, this is like six months delayed, so we're still going to do the thing. And then all of a sudden you've got 90% of your resources committed to things that don't track against your strategy. And it's a really interesting moment as a leader especially to sit there and go, well, what do we do? What do you do when you have that problem? And especially if you're a PM, you probably don't have the agency to say, scrap the entire roadmap and work on my new strategy. But at least it allows you to think about critically about whether you should be doing what you're doing and allows you to evaluate whether those things are still the most important things to work on.
turns.zh: 是啊，有很多很多时候，如果你把这个工件和流程与简化原则结合起来，通过这个过程你会开始削减很多东西，因为接下来会发生的是，假设你完成了这个练习，然后你会说，好的，我确切知道我想致力于的三个方向。然后会有一个时刻，你拿起这个策略，再看看你的路线图，它们根本不一样。路线图上充斥着各种杂乱无章的事情，比如，哦，我们因为这个原因必须做这个，或者因为那个原因必须做那个。（00:47:37）这件事我们还在做，已经延迟了六个月，所以我们还是要继续做。然后突然间，你90%的资源都投入到了与你的战略不符的事情上。这对领导者来说是一个非常有趣的时刻，尤其是要坐下来想，嗯，我们该怎么办？当你遇到这个问题时该怎么办呢？特别是如果你是一名产品经理，你可能没有权力说废掉整个路线图，转而专注于新的战略。但至少这能让你批判性地思考，你是否应该继续做你正在做的事情，以及评估这些事情是否仍然是最重要的工作方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to summarize the template real quick, and then I'm going to have another question kind of along the lines. So, if you're trying to create your own little template, you start with the mission of the business, and then I imagine you also share the mission of your team because oftentimes it's a little more specific, if you're working on it like a product team strategy. Then there's a landscape of what's happening. So, you include competitive, SWOT analysis of competition risks, product state, business state, things like that. (00:48:38): And then you share the current goals of what you're trying to achieve as a team slash business. And there's an account, honest accounting of what's happening in the product and technical hurdles and things like that that'll keep you from moving, I guess, achieving some of these goals. And then you share, here's the opportunity I see, how we win and how we actually achieve this opportunity where we place bets and things like that, or we could place bets. Then challenges of doing this, what needs to be true for this to be possible? And then you finally get to, here's what I think we should do, essentially the solution, ideally three bullet points, and then the plan. And I imagine the plan is step one, get sign off from exec. Step two, resource the team. Step three, start on this design research sprint.
turns.zh: 我会快速总结一下这个模板，然后再提出一个相关的问题。所以，如果你想创建自己的小模板，你首先要确定企业的使命，然后我猜你也会分享团队的使命，因为通常来说，在制定产品团队战略时，它会更具体一些。接下来是现状分析，包括竞争分析、SWOT分析、竞争风险、产品状态、业务状态等诸如此类的内容。（00:48:38）然后你要分享当前团队/企业试图达成的目标。接着要诚实地评估产品和技术方面的障碍，以及这些障碍如何阻碍你实现目标。然后你要分享你看到的机遇，如何取胜，以及如何抓住这些机遇，比如下赌注等。然后是挑战部分，哪些条件必须满足才能实现这些机遇。最后你要给出你的解决方案，理想情况下是三个要点，然后是计划。我猜计划的第一步是获得高管批准，第二步是为团队配备资源，第三步是开始设计研究冲刺。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Pretty much.
turns.zh: 差不多吧。

turns.en: Awesome. All right. Amazing. Somebody will create this template if you don't end up doing it.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。太好了。如果你们最终不做这个模板，总会有人会创建的。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's another-
turns.zh: 还有另外一个——

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: I hope somebody does.
turns.zh: 希望有人能做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. That'd be awesome. If they do, I will tweet it and we put it in the show notes.
turns.zh: 好的。那太棒了。如果他们做了，我会发推文，并把它放进节目笔记里。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Great.
