turns.en: So many promises already from this podcast. Along the same lines, you also have a one-pager template and process that I think people find really useful. So, how about we chat about that one briefly and then I'm going to go in a whole different direction.
turns.zh: 这一期播客已经给出了很多承诺。同样地，你们还提供了一页纸的模板和流程，我觉得大家会觉得这非常实用。所以，咱们先简单聊聊这个模板，然后我要转向一个完全不同的方向。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Okay. Yeah, I don't think I have much to say about this. That has not been said by many people many times, but whether it's a spec, a PRD, a one pager, I don't even know what else people call it. It's the document that you use to define the thing that you're doing as a product team, and that means product design, engineering, your little squad. And what I think is really useful about this process is that it's the PM's artifact. So, designers produce designs, engineers write code. What do PMs do? A lot of people might say nothing. In theory, we write at least this document and it can be a pain. I've seen lots of ways where it hasn't been done very well, but when I think it's done really well and when it's really effective is it's a tool that allows the PM to start with why. And if you structure it correctly, the most important section in my opinion in the document is the first part, which is like what is the background and context? (00:51:00): What is the problem, why does it matter and why does it matter now? And if you get those things right, the rest gets really easy, but it gives you a chance as a PM to center the team around the problem, why that problem exists, whether it's created by your own product or it's something the user is experiencing and why that problem is worth solving. That's a part that I think people sometimes forget to think about and why it's we're solving right now versus all the other problems you could be solving and then it can become the home base of the decisions that you make along the way. So, I think it's best when you have those sections and then also best when you write down on this day, we made this decision or we decided not to do this or we decided only to solve this part of the problem, not this part of the problem. Keeping a running list of that and a link off to all the different artifacts and research and things is helpful for a team.
turns.zh: 好的。是的，我觉得关于这个我没太多要说的。虽然很多人多次提及这个话题，但无论是规格说明书、产品需求文档、单页文档，还是其他叫法，我都不太清楚。总之，这份文件是产品团队用于定义产品开发方向的核心文档，涵盖产品设计、工程开发和项目组等各个环节。我认为这个流程最有价值的部分在于，它是产品经理的核心产物。设计师负责设计，工程师编写代码，那产品经理做什么？很多人可能会说产品经理什么都不做。理论上，产品经理至少要起草这份文档，而这项工作往往令人头疼。我见过很多做得很糟糕的例子，但真正出色的案例能有效引导团队围绕问题展开思考。若结构合理，文档中最重要的部分当属开头部分——背景与上下文是什么？问题是什么？为什么它重要？为什么现在必须解决？只要把这些问题理清楚，后续工作就会变得顺理成章。这部分内容往往被忽视，但它能让产品经理以问题为核心，明确问题产生的原因（无论是产品自身导致，还是用户实际遇到的痛点），以及解决该问题的价值所在。这是人们常忽略的关键思考维度，也是我们当下为何选择解决这个问题而非其他问题的核心逻辑。文档还应记录每日决策，比如“我们决定采用这个方案”、“暂不考虑某个方案”或“仅专注于解决问题中的某个维度”等。这份动态记录与各类研究资料的关联链接，对团队决策至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, just to summarize, what would be the headings again, just if someone's taking notes and wants to create the rule template?
turns.zh: 总结一下，如果有人需要制作模板，标题部分应该包括哪些内容？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: I don't think these templates have to be really complicated. It's like background and context. The problem. I would literally write why this problem matters and why this problem matters now. Don't make it complicated, just answer those questions and if you can do that, and then again, it's only really helpful if then you bring that document before you go any further to your team and you use it to have a conversation and you get the smart people around you to take shots at it. I should have mentioned this earlier with the strategy. The first person I go to is typically speaking my engineering counterpart and I say, shred this, go through it, rip it apart, vomit comments on it, tear this down how it gets better. And as a PM you can't be precious about your work. You need people to poke holes in it.
turns.zh: 我觉得这些模板不必过于复杂。比如背景与上下文、问题部分。我会直接写下“为什么这个问题重要？”以及“为什么现在必须解决这个问题？”。别搞得太复杂，只要回答好这些问题就行。另外，只有当你把这份文档拿给团队讨论，让聪明的同事们批评指正时，它才会真正发挥作用。我之前在讲策略时提到过，通常我首先会找工程师同事，让他们把文档拆解、批评、提意见，帮助改进。作为产品经理，不能对自己的工作太在意，必须接受别人的质疑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The why this matters now point is so interesting. I don't often hear that and I think it's such an important part of specs and plans and strategies because there's so many things you can do and there's certain things that are perishable that you can only do now. That if you don't do now you miss up the opportunity. And so I think that's a really interesting element that most people don't include and it reminds me of, I think I've done enough podcast episodes now where I'm just connecting all these things as people are talking. [inaudible 00:53:16] the John Nash thing happening where Karri, the founder of Linear talked about this concept of side quests as a founder. Because he's so good at staying focused and I was just like, "How do you stay focused and just get stuff done when you have so many people coming out?" He's just like, "There's the main quest and then there's the side quests and side quest I don't need to do right now. There's the main quest which is build up really successful business." And I feel like this is a good example of that in action.
turns.zh:
如今为何要关注这个问题实在太有趣了。我不常听到这种说法，但我认为这在制定规范、计划和战略时至关重要，因为有很多事情可以做，而有些事情一旦错过就无法挽回。若现在不行动，就会错失良机。所以我觉得这是大多数人未曾纳入考虑的关键要素，这让我想起自己主持的播客节目——在嘉宾发言时，我总会将各种观点串联起来。

[00:53:16的背景音]约翰·纳什（John Nash）提到的例子让我印象深刻。Linear的创始人卡里（Karri）谈到创始人需设定“主线任务”和“支线任务”。他善于保持专注，当被问及如何在众多事务中保持专注时回应道：“主线任务是打造成功的业务，支线任务可以先放一放。”这恰恰印证了这个理论在实践中的成功案例。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah, I love his take on quality and taste too.
turns.zh: 是的，我也非常欣赏他对质量和品味的见解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. What a gem.
turns.zh: 是啊，真是个难得的智慧之珠。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah, big fan of that. But yeah, I mean it's really hard to stay disciplined, it's hard to stay focused and to your point, there's a million things you could do at any given time, especially if you work at a bigger company. And so the why now is an important question to answer because if not, somebody's going to ask you. So, you may as well think about it.
turns.zh: 没错，我非常赞同他的观点。不过说真的，保持自律和专注实在不易。正如你所说，尤其是在大公司工作，随时都有无数事情要处理。所以“为何现在行动”这个问题至关重要，否则总有人会追问你原因。所以，不妨早点想清楚。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's interesting why now comes up a lot in investing in startups but rarely in product building and it feels like it should. Although I will say in the research I've done, why now ends up not being that important for startups being successful or not. So, I think there's a two sides to that coin. Anyway, I'm going to move on to a different topic and this might become a new thing that we do and I'm going to call it contrarian corner. I asked you if you have contrarian opinions about things before we started recording this episode and you had some really good ones. So, there's a couple topics I'm going to chat about and we'll see if this becomes a recurring theme and you're laughing and nodding your head, what are you thinking as I say this?
turns.zh: 是啊，有趣的是，“为何现在行动”在投资初创公司时频频被提及，但在产品开发中却鲜少被提及，而这本应是相通的。不过我研究后发现，“为何现在行动”对初创公司的成功影响并不显著。所以这事儿得辩证看。总之，我要转到另一个话题了，或许会开辟一个新栏目，叫“逆向思维角”。在录制这期节目前，我问过你们对某些事物是否有逆向看法，你们给出的观点都非常精彩。所以我会聊几个话题，看看是否能形成固定栏目。你们现在笑着点头，我说这些时你们在想什么？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: I'm thinking about when I had a podcast, you would do a show on a topic and we would click the end recording button and then every single guest would be like, I had no idea what I was doing. I made it all up, it was waterfall. None of that matters. I didn't know what I was ... People would say the wildest stuff and I would sit there as a PM and just think what. We just talked about this framework, we just talked about this thing and that's how you're supposed to do it. And then they would get off the official part and just say, yeah, it's wild. Nothing goes the way you want it to go. We're all just kind of making it up as we go. And so I hope that you get more of those takes in this part of the show.
turns.zh: 我在想自己主持播客时的情况。我们会围绕某个主题展开讨论，结束录制后，每位嘉宾都会说，我当时完全不知道自己在做什么，全凭想象，流程混乱。这些都不重要。我也不知道自己在做什么……人们会说最疯狂的想法，而作为产品经理的我只能默默想，这到底怎么回事？我们刚讨论了这个框架，刚谈了那个方法，结果实际操作时却一团乱麻。真希望在节目中能听到更多这样的见解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm very sensitive to that point right now because someone just tweeted about how they're just finding that many of my newsletter posts about how companies write product are the ideal version of what they do and I rarely or they rarely share, here's all the challenges we're having, which I think there's truth to that, but I also get into a lot of failures on this podcast. Actually, I think the podcast is a lot more of just here's things that go wrong versus the newsletter. So, I'm just like shit, I need to do more of that. So, I love that you mentioned that and let's see what we can get into. But I guess maybe before we get there, is there an example of something that didn't go just along the lines of some sort of failure slash mistake?
turns.zh: 我现在对此特别敏感，因为有人刚在推特上说，我关于公司如何写产品文案的通讯内容，往往都是理想化的版本，而现实中很少能真正做到。我很少分享这些内容，但在播客里却经常谈论失败案例。说实话，我觉得播客更多是分享失败经历，而非通讯内容。所以我现在觉得，天哪，我得多分享些失败案例了。很高兴你提到这个问题，让我们深入探讨一下。不过在深入之前，有没有例子能说明产品开发过程中遇到的失败或错误？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: I might be foreshadowing, but a question I ask in every product interview is what's the worst product you've ever shipped? And that's because I don't think you're a good PM if you haven't shipped something that's really shitty, you just haven't had enough reps, you haven't done it enough time. And it's not only that you've done it but that you can admit it and which one it is. That's so important. And I remember, it was so dumb, I'm still so mad about this, that we did this. I won't name which team, which company, I'm not going to call that out, but we decided we needed to do a rewrite, red flag number one of a existing product and engineer who I'd worked with many times. We had a really good relationship and this person was like, yeah, yeah, it's going to take six months, no problem. (00:56:47): Core part of the product been around for forever. One of those things that the code is still, it's still the code written by the founders kind of thing. It didn't take six months, it took two and a half years. It still wasn't done. It almost never, it went on for so much longer than it should have. It took us forever to get to feature parody. It was the worst project. So, many people rotated in and out of it. Everyone thought it was dumb, sunk cost fallacy, just the worst. And it's because A, we got arrogant and we thought we could do it. B, we skipped discovery. We didn't really write a one-pager, we just went for it. We didn't do enough technical and design research into what the requirements would actually have to be. And there you have it.
turns.zh: 我可能在暗示，但我在每次产品面试中都会问一个问题：你推出的最糟糕的产品是什么？因为我认为，如果你没有推出过真正糟糕的产品，那你就不是一个优秀的产品经理。你只是缺乏足够的经验，尝试次数不够。而关键不在于你是否推出了产品，而在于你能否承认失败并指出问题所在。这点至关重要。我记得有个例子，真是太蠢了，至今想起来还是气不打一处。我们决定重写一个现有产品，这个人我合作过很多次，是个很棒的工程师。他一开始说没问题，六个月搞定。结果花了两年半还没完成。核心功能部分僵持了太久，代码还是创始人写的，根本没达到预期。最终我们花了无数时间才实现基本功能。这真是最失败的项目了。很多人参与其中又离开，大家都觉得这项目太蠢，陷入沉没成本谬论，简直糟糕透顶。原因在于：A、我们太自大，认为自己能搞定；B、我们跳过了探索阶段。根本没写需求文档，直接上手，没有充分调研技术和设计需求。就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And did not work out or was it a huge success in the end and it changed the trajectory of the business?
turns.zh: 那最后结果如何？是大获成功还是彻底失败，改变了公司发展轨迹？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Absolutely not. But you know what, I didn't get fired, so it's fine.
turns.zh: 绝对失败。不过好在我没被炒鱿鱼，还算幸运。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like I've gone through those experiences and then three, four years later it's like another, maybe this rewrite and redesign may work because we haven't updated this thing in a long time.
turns.zh: 我感觉自己也经历过类似的经历，三年四年后，可能再来一次重写或重新设计，但实际上我们早就该更新那个产品了。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Just don't do it. Don't rewrite. If anyone ever tells you to do a rewrite, don't do it. A side by side re-write, nope.
turns.zh: 千万别重写。任何人让你重写，都别答应。那种一对一的对比重写，千万别做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, what I run into is once you get too far down a redesign slash rewrite everyone's building in that new world and then you launch an experiment's negative and then it's just like, oh, we just got to launch it. We're going to claw back. We're going to get figure out how to get back to neutral someday.
turns.zh: 是啊，我遇到的情况是一旦你深入到重新设计或重写阶段，每个人都在新世界里开发，然后实验失败了，结果只能硬着头皮上线，再想办法回归正轨。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah. Don't do that.
turns.zh: 是啊，可别那么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Good times. Okay, well maybe we'll start a failure corner. That could be a new segment. We may have a little sound and theme music, but this time we have contrarian corner and you have a couple contrarian opinions about a couple topics. The first is product management. What is something that you believe about product management that maybe other people are less convinced by?
turns.zh: 真是有趣的时光。好吧，或许我们可以开设一个“失败角”栏目。这会是个新板块。我们可能需要配上点音效和主题音乐，但这次我们要打造一个“反向思维角”，大家可以就几个话题分享些不同见解。第一个话题是产品管理。关于产品管理，你有什么观点是其他人不太认同的？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: The one I like to have in this area is that people who are really excited about being data-driven, to me that is oftentimes a red flag for their product thinking, especially if it's an executive who's saying things like, oh, so we make all our decisions with our dashboards. To me that says that the team is over-emphasizing quantitative data at the expense of qualitative data and they're not using good judgment. They probably don't do a lot of direct user research. They don't really understand the humans who are using the thing, what they need, what they care about, and they're managing via a dashboard. And maybe if they got really, really good at picking metrics, it would be fine. And oftentimes maybe it is fine. Maybe you have a high volume business that's really easy to run experiments on and that works for you. But most PMs, most jobs, most products, you're going to be better off talking to 10 users and you'll get more and better insights out of why things are happening than you would with any dashboard.
turns.zh: 我在这方面特别想说的是，很多对数据驱动特别狂热的人，在我看来，这往往是他们产品思维的警示信号，尤其是当是高管说出“我们所有决策都基于仪表板数据”这种话时。这说明团队过度依赖定量数据，却忽视了定性数据，没有运用良好的判断力。他们可能根本不做用户调研，完全不了解产品用户的需求和痛点，只是靠仪表板来管理产品。或许他们如果能精通指标选择，倒也无妨。但大多数情况下，这么做未必有效。可能你所在的公司业务量大、实验成本低，这种策略对他们适用。但对于大多数产品经理、多数职位和多数产品而言，与10位用户交流会比依赖仪表板更有收获，能获得更深刻的洞察，理解产品背后的逻辑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, the takeaway there is just be careful when someone is saying they're super data-driven. Our team is super data-driven or company company's super data-driven.
turns.zh: 所以，关键是当有人自诩“数据驱动”时，要保持警惕。比如团队自诩“数据驱动”或者公司号称如此。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah, and maybe it's true and that's great. I am not saying that you don't need data. You absolutely do need to instrument your products and understand if it's working at scale, but you can't forget that, you need to know why. It won't tell you why anything is happening. If you don't understand why it's happening, I don't think you can come up with good insights about what you should do next. One quick story on this. I remember really early on in my career, Adam Medros, who was a VP [inaudible 01:00:24] at TripAdvisor, we were in a room, just had this meeting called product review that was amazing when I first joined and someone was justifying this project and he just, I hope he is okay with me saying this because this is my memory of this moment. (01:00:38): He was just like, this is an obviously better thing. Just do it. Stop. Stop it. Stop doing all the stuff that you're doing. Stop with these numbers, whatever it was that they were doing, if it's obviously better, if it's logically better, use your good judgment and do that thing and let's move on. And I've always thought about that, but you can just do the obviously better thing.
turns.zh: 是啊，或许他们说得没错，这固然好。但我不是说你不需要数据。当然需要对产品进行数据监测，了解其大规模应用效果，但别忘了更重要的是理解其背后的逻辑。数据无法解释事件发生的深层原因。如果你不理解因果关系，就无法得出有效的洞察。说个小故事。我记得职业生涯早期，在TripAdvisor担任VP的亚当·梅德罗斯（Adam Medros）参加产品评审会时，有人试图为某个项目辩护。他说：这显然是个更好的方案，直接去做吧。停下。别再纠结数据了。如果方案明显更优、逻辑更清晰，就用你的判断力去推进吧。这个时刻让我印象深刻，但我一直认为，有时候确实该直接选择明显更好的方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I love that I pull that card sometimes, but I think you almost have to do it that way of just like, okay, everyone, this one's just obviously a good idea. Let's just do it. Enough research. Okay, another topic that you have some interesting opinions about his product content very close to our hearts, both my heart and your heart. Do share.
turns.zh: 是啊，我有时也会搬出这张牌，但我觉得必须采取这种方式：好吧，大家，这事儿显然没问题。直接做吧。别再调研了。好吧，还有个你很有见解的话题——产品内容。这对我们双方都意义非凡。请分享一下你的观点。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Really if you're going to make good content, you have to sanitize and frameworkize the thing that you're working on. And then slowly, I think for a lot of people who are reading it and looking at it, their thinking starts to become, well look how well I did this framework. Look how well I implemented this thing. And they lose touch with the point which is creating impact. And so all of this content makes it really noisy and then makes people think that, oh, if I just do these things that I'll get what I want. And now I'll just check off my list and then I checked it off and then I should get my promotion at the end of the day. But it's like the best PMs have built up so many different frameworks and they can apply them in different ways. And then sometimes they throw them out and they say, nothing I have in my toolkit makes sense for this moment, but I know what to do because I have intuition and I have data and I've talked to users or whatever. (01:02:16): And so content sometimes can get in the way of the impact because you're trying to apply it and you think that the point is the framework and the point is the one pager or whatever it is that you're doing when it's not. And then if you're a leader and maybe if you've had the good and ill fortune of having published content, someone comes to you and says, well, you said in that one podcast episode that you don't believe in roadmaps, so why are you asking me for a roadmap? And then you're the who's sitting there being like, well, it's a little more complicated than that. And that was a fun take that I had, but I actually need to understand what we're doing because planning and I need to figure out what my budget is, blah, blah, blah.
turns.zh:
老实说，如果你想创作优质内容，就必须对自己正在做的事情进行精简和框架化处理。然后，我觉得很多读者和观众会开始思考：看看我这框架做得多好，看看我这功能实现得多棒。然而他们却忽视了最初的目标——创造影响力。于是所有这些内容就变得冗余，让人们误以为只要照着模板做就能达成目标。最后他们只是在勾选任务清单，却始终得不到想要的晋升机会。

（01:02:16）：优秀的产品经理会积累大量框架，并能灵活运用。有时他们会抛弃旧框架，坦言：现在这个场景用不上这些工具，但我凭借直觉、数据和用户反馈就能找到正确的解决方案。

（02:01:28）：有时内容反倒成了阻碍，因为人们试图套用模板，却忽视了核心要点——框架只是工具，关键在于用数据和洞察力去解决问题。当领导者被追问：你不是说不信路线图吗？那为什么还要让我写路线图？你只能尴尬地解释：实际情况更复杂……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so funny that I didn't think about you as a leader having put stuff out that people put back at you. And I think your point about one for you, for people to consume content online about how to do product management, you have to really distill it. And to your point, it often loses the nuance. Because if you had all the ones, no one's going to even read it so complicated and long. And then the other point of there's also just it has to be interesting. So, if it's another just like, here's how a roadmap really is successfully and it's like what everyone's already done, no one's going to read it. So, you always have to have a new take. And with that comes, it's not actually always true. I just wanted people to react to this idea.
turns.zh: 太有趣了，我从没想过你也会遇到被质疑的情况。关于产品管理内容，你提到要精简易懂，避免冗长。这点很对，但用户往往忽略细节。比如长篇大论的路线图教程，根本没人会看。必须保持趣味性，让读者有共鸣。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah, I mean it's helpful. I think there's some people who create, I mean there's many things at my last role, we all had your newsletter and we listened to the show and then people would bring, I should have found a clip, but I can't remember, there were a couple of moments where we would listen to a piece of it or find an article and say, oh, this could help. Or what if we did it that way? I think there was a newsletter article about Figma and they had some templates. They're like product review template for FigJam. Love that one. Use that one all the time.
turns.zh: 确实很有帮助。我记得在上家公司，大家都订阅你的邮件、听你的播客。有人会拿出某个片段，比如关于Figma的模板文章，应用到FigJam的产品评审中。这种案例太棒了，我们常用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: So, yeah, I mean the stuff's really useful. It's just like you have to be smart about when you apply it. And then if you're a leader and there's all this content available, you have to know why you're not following the rules.
turns.zh: 是的，这些内容确实实用。但关键在于何时该套用，何时该创新。作为领导者，面对海量内容时，必须清楚为何要打破常规。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If they're just like, hey, look at this newsletter post letting you write, we should be doing it this way. Versus I think people assume these are the one way to do it or innately will work at your company. And I really like your point, which maybe counter to what I do, but I think it's an important nuance that I feel like I should add to every newsletters. This isn't necessarily going to work at your company. Sometimes the culture is different and this won't fit or this isn't a complete version. As much as I try to give people, here's everything you need to do this thing well, there's always a little bit missing
turns.zh: 他们可能只是说，嘿，看看这篇时事通讯帖子，里面教你如何写作，我们应该也照这个方法做。但人们往往误以为这就是唯一的正确做法，或者默认它在你的公司就能奏效。我很赞同你的观点——虽然这可能与我的做法相悖，但我认为这是一个重要的细微差别，值得我在每期时事通讯中强调。这种方法未必适用于你的公司。有时公司文化不同，难以落地，或者这套方案并非完整的解决方案。即便我尽力为大家提供做好这件事所需的全部要素，总还是会遗漏些关键点。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: And I think if you don't have that context, it can be a little demoralizing like, well, how am I ever going to do that thing that they get to do at this magical company? But again, if you view it as more like here all the tools that you can add to your toolkit and you pull them out when you're in a situation from which they can be useful, that's how I think about it. Versus this is the one way to do it like you said, the only way you can write a one page or the only way you can write an experiment, it's more like you can do it in many different ways.
turns.zh: 我觉得如果没有这种背景知识，可能会让人有点沮丧，比如，天哪，他们在那家神奇的公司里能做到那些事，我怎么可能也做到呢？但话说回来，如果你把这看作是可以扩充自己技能库的工具——在需要时随时拿出来使用——我觉得这才是正确的思路。而不是那种“这就是唯一正确的做法”之类的说法。就像你说的，写一页纸的提案或者设计实验，可能有无数种方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I find myself, I'm not actually, I rarely tell people here's the way to do it. Usually what I try to describe is here's how the best companies do it, as much as I can get into and leave it to the reader to decide is this going to be a fit for me, should I try to implement it? But still, I think there's an implication. This is the way to do research, here's the way to do roadmap, here's the way to prioritize. But I think it's interesting that you also, yourself create a lot of content and you actually found a lot of value from being, let's not call you content creator because I don't like being labeled as a creator myself.
turns.zh: 我发现自己很少直接告诉别人应该怎么做。通常我会尽可能详细地描述顶尖公司的做法，让读者自己判断是否适合自己，是否值得尝试。但这种思路确实存在暗示。比如，研究应该这样做，路线图应该这样制定，优先级排序应该这样处理。不过有趣的是，你自己也创作了很多内容，并且从中获得了很大价值。虽然我不喜欢被贴上“内容创作者”的标签，但还是要说，你确实是个很棒的内容创作者。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Someone one's called me a product influencer and I'll died like a little bit.
turns.zh: 有人称我为“产品影响者”，我当时简直激动得不行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's how I feel. I'd love to hear just the impact you've seen from spending time creating podcasts and blog posts and tweeting about really great stuff because a lot of people are thinking about investing in this stuff.
turns.zh: 这就是我的感受。我很想听听你通过创作播客、博客文章和推特分享优质内容所产生的影响，毕竟很多公司都在考虑投入这类资源。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah, it's probably the best thing I've ever done for my career and I am so grateful for the people whose idea it was, who supported me and especially at Drift, when that became such a part of what we were doing at that time. And it's been helpful for a couple of reasons. One is just networking and access. I probably wouldn't be here today if I hadn't done that and if a friend of a friend had read the thing, it's like it just creates so many more connections. And so access to people and networking is one of the first benefits. (01:06:51): Also building a personal brand is really helpful if you want, one of the things that I always wanted to do with my career is try to make it so that I'm always employable. I just didn't want to, I'm an 08 grad not to put my age out there, and it was a hard time. And so I've always had this in the back of my mind, you want to be able to have a solid career. And so I thought that investing in my personal brand would be a way to help me get access to roles. It helps in recruiting as well when I'm trying to hire people. Because a lot of my job now is bringing people in and because I've been vocal about how I like to work and who I am, a lot of people and they will send me a note and say, I want to work with you, or I want to work on a team like that. (01:07:35): And that's huge because if my job is to hire people, then that's great and people can get a sense of who I am without needing to be on the phone with me. My favorite benefit outside of those things has been that it's helped me learn more from the work I've done than I otherwise would've been able to. Because in order to make content, you have to think through what you did, you have to summarize it, process it, make it interesting for people. And then especially if it's in a podcast meeting, talk to somebody about it. And the process of doing that means that you're paying attention to what you're learning along the way. And so often we don't do that because we're busy working, we have our lives, things are happening. And that to me is, I think what's made me a better product person faster is because I spent the time to think about what I was doing in a way that I wouldn't have if I didn't have to write something down.
turns.zh:
是啊，这大概是我职业生涯中做过的最棒的事，我非常感激那些提出这个想法、支持我的人——尤其是Drift团队，当时这项工作已然成为我们当时工作的核心部分。它带来了诸多益处：首先是人脉拓展和资源获取。如果没有参与这项工作，我今天大概不会站在这里；如果不是朋友的朋友读了那篇文章，我也不会获得如此多的机会。获取人脉和资源无疑是首要的收获。

（01:06:51）此外，若想在职业生涯中保持竞争力，我认为投资个人品牌建设至关重要。我是2008届毕业生（不方便透露年龄），当时就业形势严峻。于是我始终将个人品牌建设视为职业生涯的核心支柱。通过个人品牌塑造，我不仅能获得更多职位机会，在招聘时也更具说服力。因为我现在的工作职责之一就是招募人才，而当我公开分享工作理念和个人风格时，许多求职者会主动联系我，表示希望加入这样的团队。

（01:07:35）最宝贵的收获在于，个人品牌建设让我能比以往更深入地反思工作历程。在创作内容时，必须系统梳理工作经验、提炼核心要点并使其趣味横生。尤其是在播客会议中与他人讨论时，整个思考过程迫使我持续关注自身成长的点滴。相反，日常工作中我们常因忙碌或分心而忽视这些关键反思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that comes across in your content that you've somehow figured out is to avoided being cringy and very thirsty for followers. And I think when a lot of people here build a personal brand, it's like, I don't want to.
turns.zh: 从你的内容中能感受到，你成功避开了那种令人尴尬、急切追逐粉丝的套路。我觉得很多本地人士在打造个人品牌时，总会想：我不想这样做。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: I know. It makes me ill even saying that, it's like too gross.
turns.zh: 我懂。光是说出来都让我难受，太恶心了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I never thought of it or wanted to think of it that way. And I'm just curious what advice you'd give to people that want to go down this route without feeling, I guess one, is just feeling like they're being cringey, and two, avoiding content people be like, oh my God, I can't believe this stuff [inaudible 01:09:02].
turns.zh: 我从未这样想过，也不想这样想。我很好奇，对于那些想走这条路却又不想陷入尴尬境地的人，你会给出什么建议？比如，一是避免尴尬；二是避免内容让人觉得"天哪，这也太离谱了"（01:09:02处语音模糊）。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah, the clickbait tweet thread situation. I think the step one's going to be cringe. Your first 10, 20, however many posts are going to be bad. I would imagine if you went back and listened to your first episode, you would be cringing just because you've learned so much since then. Right?
turns.zh: 是啊，比如那种标题党推特话题的情况。第一步肯定会很尴尬。前十条、二十条帖子都会很糟糕。我敢打赌，如果你现在回听自己的第一期播客，肯定会觉得尴尬，因为你自那以后进步太大了。对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: It's natural.
turns.zh: 这很正常。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Although randomly the first episode ever is the most popular episode. So, with [inaudible 01:09:29], which I could see why it was so popular.
turns.zh: 尽管首集播出时反响平平，但它却意外地成了最受欢迎的一集。所以，就拿[听不清 01:09:29]来说，能理解它为何如此受欢迎。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: So, it went really hot with your first guest.
turns.zh: 第一位嘉宾的互动确实非常热烈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's right. That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。没错。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: So, yeah, first get over the fact that it's going to be cringe. It's going to be cringe. Like anything, you just have to get started and it'll fade away eventually and you don't have to think about it. Two B, this is such gross advice, but you have to be authentic. It has to be real. And I think what came through in the show that I did was those were my real questions that I was really working on. (01:09:59): So, we joked about how we would turn off the recording and then we would get the real story, but I would turn the recording off and I would say, okay, we talked about this thing. Here's actually happening in my job today, what would you do? And so those were real questions that I had, real processes that I was working on and real advice that I needed at that time. And I think that's why it was valuable is because I was actively a PM and the way that I'm still actively in product, that was always something that I wanted because it meant that the content had to be relevant for me and wasn't just for likes and share.
turns.zh: 所以，首先要接受这种尴尬感是不可避免的。这种尴尬感迟早会消失，最终你会习惯它，不必刻意去在意。说个难听点儿的，这建议太烂了，但你必须保持真实。内容必须真实可信。我在节目中呈现的自我，正是那些我真正在思考的问题。（01:09:59）：我们曾开玩笑说，关掉录音机就能听到真实的故事，但我每次都会关掉录音机，然后问：好吧，我们刚聊到这个事儿。今天我工作中遇到的真实情况，你会怎么做？这些都是我真实面临的问题，正在解决的难题，以及当时急需的建议。我觉得这档节目之所以有价值，正是因为我当时还是一名产品经理，而我至今仍活跃在产品领域。这意味着内容必须与我的实际工作相关，而不是为了博眼球和传播量而生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think there's some two really important points there that stood out to me. One is your stuff's going to be terrible if you don't actually have any background or experience in the things, you're just pretending. It's like you're acting like someone that knows about this thing, but you don't actually. And so I think that's an incredibly important part of this is don't try to become an online creator person if you haven't done the thing, because people will see that you don't know what you're really talking about and you'll run out of stuff and it'll be like, okay, well I did it for two months and I have nothing more to say.
turns.zh: 这里有两点让我印象深刻。第一，如果你对某个领域没有背景或经验，内容注定会糟糕透顶。你只是在假装懂行，却实则一窍不通。第二，如果你没有亲身实践过某个领域，就别试图成为网络创作者。人们会看穿你的虚伪，内容枯竭后只能无奈放弃。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then the other piece is there's a guest who shared this quote that has stuck with me from Einstein, which is something like, "Seek not to be successful but of value." And I find that that's a really good framing for sharing stuff is just share things that are interesting to you and useful and come at it from this is useful, not from, I'm trying to build a following. Because people can tell if that's the-
turns.zh: 还有一点，嘉宾分享了爱因斯坦的一句话，让我深有共鸣：“不要追求成功，而要追求有价值。” 我认为这句话为内容分享提供了绝佳框架——分享真正感兴趣且有用的内容，出发点应该是内容本身的价值，而非为了积累粉丝。人们能轻易辨别出你是否真心在创作，还是在迎合大众。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah, people can absolutely tell. And the other thing is there's a little bit of too cool for school mixed in here and there are definitely people who will tell you your content is cringe or make fun of you or whatever because that's what they want to do. And I'm not even going to get into psychology of that, but people will do that. And I've always been of the mind that the really interesting people out there, people who are unashamedly interested in stuff and who are like, yeah, I'm nerding out about this and I'm sharing it because I'm interested in it. And for better for worse, I love working in product. I love the job. (01:12:08): Even all the gross stuff you have to do, it's super interesting. You meet really cool people, you get to ship stuff, you get to see the stuff get used by people and solve problems. It's a really cool job and I've always been interested in how to do it better and it doesn't matter to me that some people might think that's cringe because that's cool, but this is what I do all day long, so I'd like to get better at it.
turns.zh: 是啊，人家肯定能看出来。另外，这里还夹杂着一种"自命不凡"的意味，总会有人说你的内容很尴尬、嘲笑你之类的，因为他们就是想这么做。我甚至都不想深究其心理机制，但人们就是会这么做。我一直认为，那些真正有趣的人——那些毫不掩饰地对某件事感兴趣、会说"我对这个很着迷，所以要分享出来"的人——无论结果好坏，我都热爱产品工作。我热爱这份职业。（01:12:08）：即使你得做些讨厌的事，也非常有趣。你能结识很酷的人，参与产品发布，看到产品被人们使用并解决问题。这真是一份很棒的工作。我一直想如何把它做得更好，即使有些人觉得这很尴尬，但这很酷，因为这是我每天的工作，所以我想把它做得更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's such a big part of it. I didn't even mention that. Just it needs to feel really authentic and clearly for you is just like, there's just stuff I want to share because it's really interesting to me.
turns.zh: 我觉得这很重要。我甚至都没提到这一点。关键是内容得真实自然，对你来说，就是“有些东西我很想分享，因为它们对我来说真的很有趣”。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The way I actually started writing was exactly the two reasons you just shared. One is I wanted to learn the thing and so writing helped me figure things out. And then two is I just thought it was interesting and I found it useful and I just assumed other people might find it useful. So, I did also learn, and I wonder if you found this too, is that you think the things are not going to be that interesting or useful to people, so basic for you, but people find the most basic stuff so interesting. Because there's always more to learn about how to roadmap, how to prioritize, how to hire, how to talk, to have difficult conversations, performance review.
turns.zh: 我真正开始写作的原因正是你刚刚提到的两个原因。一是我想学习相关知识，所以写作帮助我理清思路；二是我觉得内容很有趣、很有用，就想其他人可能也会觉得有用。比如，我确实学到了东西，不知道你有没有同感，就是你可能觉得某些东西对别人来说太基础、太无聊，但人们却觉得这些最基础的东西很有趣。比如，关于路线图规划、优先级排序、招聘、沟通、困难对话、绩效评估，总有更多东西可以学习。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: All of that is absolutely true. And I think one of the first pieces of content that I was really happy with was I was working with somebody and they were making a PowerPoint presenter slides or whatever, and I just wrote out in my notebook like, okay, here's how I do that. I start with an outline on paper and then I draw little boxes for the slides and I write out the headline of the slides. And then once I have a tight outline and I have the literal text that will go across the top of each of those things, then I sketch out how I want the slides to go. And then I go into Google Docs and I actually make the slide. (01:13:51): And it was like some silly little thing and this person sat there and said, holy, you just totally changed the way I did this and this took me 75% less time than it would've taken me otherwise. And I was like, I may do this dumb drawing. Why is this a big deal? And yeah, that's when I realized that the stuff that's easy for you might be a stuff that is most interesting because it's something that maybe you're really good at that you don't realize.
turns.zh: 这一切都千真万确。我记得我第一次写的比较满意的内容，是和别人合作做PPT演示文稿时，我在笔记本上写下：好的，我会这样做。先在纸上列大纲，再为每个幻灯片画小框，写下标题。等大纲确定，标题也写好后，再画出幻灯片的布局。然后用Google Docs把幻灯片做出来。（01:13:51）：这只是个小技巧，但那个人坐下来说，天哪，你彻底改变了我的做法，比我之前省了75%的时间。我就想，我只是画了张图而已，这有什么大不了的？那时我意识到，对你来说简单的事物，可能对别人来说最有趣，因为这或许正是你擅长却未曾意识到的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think people need to really internalize that point. If there's something that you're doing that you consistently find useful and works often, that is going to be really useful for someone to hear. So, that could be a good place to start. Maggie, we've gone through everything that I was hoping to get through and more, which is awesome.
turns.zh: 我觉得大家真的需要深刻理解这一点。如果你正在做某件事，并且发现它确实有用、经常奏效，那么分享给别人听会很有帮助。这或许是个不错的切入点。玛吉，我们已经讨论完了所有我希望探讨的内容，甚至超出了预期，这太棒了。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 太好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before we get to a very exciting lightning round, is there anything else that you want to share or touch on think might be useful to leave folks with?
turns.zh: 在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，还有什么你想分享或提及的，觉得对大家有帮助的？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: My hope is always that people listen to stuff like this and realize that it's messier than you think you can fail a lot and still be successful and that they should have fun. I think that gets missed in a lot of the product content is like, have fun, enjoy it. People are weird, people do weird stuff and you build stuff for people, which it makes it all very entertaining. So, I've always found a lot of joy in the job.
turns.zh: 我一直希望大家听完这些内容后，能意识到事情比你想象的更复杂——你可能会多次失败，但最终仍能成功。最重要的是，要享受这个过程。我觉得很多产品内容都忽略了这一点：要玩得开心，享受过程。人都是奇怪的，人们会做出奇怪的事，而你要为人们开发产品，这一切就变得非常有趣。所以，我在这份工作中一直能找到很多乐趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And to your point of carrying the water as a PM where you're kind of doing all the things, it's like you can create that fun. You can make the team your own fun and change the culture, create the culture. I find that so underappreciated for PM.
turns.zh: 至于你提到的产品经理要当“救火队员”，什么都得管——其实你可以创造这种乐趣。你可以让团队自得其乐，改变团队文化，塑造团队文化。我发现这一点在产品经理群体中被严重低估了。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, well with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好的，现在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节。大家准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: I'm ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maggie, what are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 玛吉，你向别人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: First, most common one is probably the Presentation Secrets of Steve Jobs, the little tiny one, really great way to improve your speaking skills and your presentation skills and to get distracted executives to agree with the point you're making. So, that's one. Thinking in Bets by Annie Duke is the second one. Coming back to the point about being able to make bets, I think that one's a really interesting one. And then bonus third one, this is more like a desk reference that I now have on my desk, the Scaling People book by Claire Hughes Johnson. I really enjoyed the way that one is working and it just sits on my desk and I reference it every once in a while, especially as manager.
turns.zh: 首先，最常见的可能是《史蒂夫·乔布斯的演讲秘诀》，那本很薄的小书，真的能大大提升你的演讲技巧和展示能力，让那些心不在焉的高管也认同你的观点。这是第一本。安妮·杜克的《思考的赌局》是第二本。回到如何下注这个话题，我觉得这本书非常有趣。第三本推荐是克莱尔·休斯·约翰逊的《人才倍增法则》。这本书现在就放在我的书桌上，用起来很方便，特别是作为管理者时，我时不时会翻阅参考。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have it both under my laptop right where I'm sitting and then also way behind there and it's one of the most popular episodes I've done with Claire, so if folks haven't listened to that one. Highly recommend. She's incredible. Great choice. What is a favorite recent movie or TV show you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 我的笔记本电脑下方就放着这本书，后面还有一本。这是我和克莱尔合作过的最受欢迎的节目之一，如果大家还没听过的话，强烈推荐。她太棒了。选得好。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Okay, so my husband is in the industry, as we say here in LA, and so we watch a lot of good and bad shows in TV, but I think my favorite one that I've watched recently was Slow Horses. Gary Oldman is incredible. Highly recommend.
turns.zh: 好的，我丈夫在洛杉矶的这个行业，所以我们看了很多电视节目，有好有坏。但我最近最喜欢看的是《慢马》。加里·奥尔德曼太棒了。强烈推荐。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I haven't heard that one yet. Good tip. What is a favorite interview question you really like to ask which I think you already gave away, but let's touch on it again.
turns.zh: 哇，我还没听过这部剧呢。好建议。你最喜欢问的一个面试问题是什么？虽然你之前已经提到过，但还是再聊聊吧。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: I did. Yeah, it is what is the worst product that you've ever shipped? I think the best answers are ones, and I don't even care if someone listens to this and then I do this in an interview, people immediately laugh a little bit. They remember the horrible thing they did and then they share that horrible thing with you. And it tells me you have some humor, you're humble and you can point out when you've made a mistake. You've done enough to be able to confidently say, of course I've made a mistake. Because none of us are perfect. And you know how to spot those mistakes and you can learn from them. And I've always found that those conversations are the most interesting.
turns.zh: 我提到过。是这样的，你问过的最好的问题之一是：“你推出的最失败的产品是什么？” 我觉得最好的回答是那些坦诚的人，甚至当我把这个问题用在采访中时，人们都会笑一笑。他们会回忆起自己做过的糟糕事，然后分享给你。这显示出你的幽默感、谦逊，以及能承认错误的勇气。你已经足够自信地说，“当然我犯过错，毕竟人无完人。” 你能识别出这些错误，并从中吸取教训。我发现这样的对话最有意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 你最近发现的最喜欢的产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: One because I've seen you on Twitter, you're a future fit guy.
turns.zh: 因为我在推特上看到过，你是个未来健身达人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I'm.
turns.zh: 是啊，我是。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Is that correct?
turns.zh: 对吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I use it three times a week. I love it.
turns.zh: 我每周用三次。我很喜欢。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Yes. I was also a future fit person. I think it's great. It's a great product. I'm now on Ladder Fit.
turns.zh: 是的。我以前也是个未来健身达人。我觉得这产品很棒。我现在用Ladder Fit。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've heard of that.
turns.zh: 听说过。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: And personally, I love not being, I don't have to talk to the coach every day. I don't need the accountability, so that's not a thing that I needed as an ex athlete. So, for me, that didn't serve me and I like the anonymity of it and it comes with a totally unhinged group chat for your whole team. It's fantastic. I'm really enjoying it.
turns.zh: 对我个人来说，我不喜欢每天和教练交流，不需要那种监督，所以作为前运动员，我不需要那种模式。对我来说，那种模式没用，我喜欢它的匿名性，还附带一个整个团队的疯狂群聊。太棒了。我真的很喜欢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet.
turns.zh: 不错。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: So, that's one more of a funny one. And the second one, not to get real niche, but I think good products are products that are focused. They do one thing incredibly well and they're not, to your point about side quest, there's no side quests. I'm a new mom. There's this app called Pump Log. I have never seen an execute so well on one problem. There's not a single thing where I think, oh, I wish it did this. It does it. It's like I paid $14 for it. I've never paid for an app like that in my life.
turns.zh: 好的，这又是个有趣的故事。第二个观点是，别追求太小众的产品，但我认为好的产品必须专注于某一件事。它们在某个特定领域做到极致。就像你说的支线任务，根本没有那些东西。我刚当了妈妈，有个叫Pump Log的应用。我从没见过哪款产品能如此精准地解决一个问题，没有任何让我后悔的地方。它就该这样，我花14美元买的，这辈子从没为类似应用花过钱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I'm downloading it right after we finish. Do you have a favorite life motto that you either repeat yourself, often like to share with folks, find useful, and just kind of living life?
turns.zh: 好的，等我们结束后我马上就下载。你有没有一条生活格言，既能反复自述，又喜欢与人分享，觉得很有用，还能融入日常生活？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: I'm sure there's mottos' I could say that would be aspirational mottos', but the real one is if it's worth doing, it's worth doing well. And again, from being in sports to going to school to being in product, in my opinion, if you're going to do something, do it to the best of your ability because that's what you do with your day. You spend so much time working, you may as well be good at it or trying to get good at it. And that's always how I've lived my life.
turns.zh: 我肯定能说出一些励志格言，但真正实用的是：如果值得做，就要做好。无论是运动、求学还是产品开发，在我看来，既然要做，就要竭尽全力做到最好，因为这决定了你一天的价值。既然要投入大量时间工作，不如把它做得出色，或者努力做到出色。这就是我的人生信条。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I so love that message. I always think about that. Final question, you are an Olympic speed skater, which I don't think people would know necessarily. That's insane. My question is there some bad speed skating that would surprise people that would be like, what?
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个理念了。我经常思考这个问题。最后一个问题，你是奥运会速滑选手，我想很多人可能不知道。这太不可思议了。我的问题是，有没有一些糟糕的速滑经历，让人惊讶得想说：什么？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Ooh, that is one I've never been asked before. The whole experience, I've obviously learned a ton from it, and I think what might surprise people about being a small sport athlete is that you have to think in four or eight year chunks. And so it's one of those things where you grind for so long in a dark corner and then you get a chance to get the light to shine on you and you learn how to love the process. Especially for speed skating, I was a long track speed skater, it's a 400-meter rink. (01:20:15): You just are always turning left and going in a circle. There's not a lot going on. It's just you and your thoughts and you just really, really learn how to get good at perfecting something over and over again, and you learn how to grind, you learn how to focus, and I think it's also cool you get to go superfast. But yeah, I don't know if that would surprise people about speed skating, but I think just about being a small sport elite athlete, it's really about years and years and years of toiling and silence to get maybe one shot at something great.
turns.zh: 哦，这个问题我从没被问过。整个经历让我收获颇丰。作为小众体育项目的运动员，最令人惊讶的是你必须以四年或八年的周期规划。就像在黑暗角落埋头苦干很久，突然迎来聚光灯照耀的时刻。你学会热爱这个过程。特别是速滑，我是长道速滑选手，赛道400米。（01:20:15）你只是一圈圈地左转，几乎没什么花样。就是你和自己的思绪作斗争，不断磨砺技艺，学会专注。我觉得能跑得超快也很酷。但我不确定这对速滑是否有启发，但对于小众体育项目的精英运动员来说，就是年复一年地默默耕耘，只为争取一次登上大舞台的机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, much of what you just said would apply 100% to product management and I love that. Maggie, you are awesome. Two final questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and maybe ask you any follow-up questions, and then two, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 你刚刚说的很多观点完全适用于产品管理，我太赞同了。Maggie，你太棒了。最后两个问题。如果听众想联系你，或者有后续问题，哪里能找到你？第二个问题，听众如何能为你提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: You can find me on Twitter for sure. By LinkedIn, but just speaking of cringe, I just can't get into LinkedIn posting.
turns.zh: 你肯定能在Twitter上找到我。至于LinkedIn，说实话我实在没法适应那个平台的发帖模式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: LinkedIn's gotten better, I'd give it a shot. It's actually pretty interesting now, which sound weird to say.
turns.zh: LinkedIn现在改进了很多，我觉得值得一试。现在它其实挺有趣的，说起来挺奇怪的。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Thinking about it, I better go back to work in a couple of weeks and thinking about LinkedIn. But yeah, Twitter for sure, LinkedIn for sure, and I've always tried to be helpful to other people, so I don't have an answer for how people can be helpful to me, my goal is really to share what I've been doing, the rooms that I get to be in, the access to the content and the people and the learning that I've had. So, hopefully I can find ways to keep sharing that.
turns.zh: 仔细想想，几周后我最好还是回去工作，再说说领英（LinkedIn）。不过推特（Twitter）肯定还是要用的，领英也不能落下。我一直致力于帮助他人，但对于别人如何能帮到我，我还真没想好答案。我的目标就是分享自己近期的经历、参与的项目、获取的内容资源、结识的人脉以及从中获得的学习收获。希望能找到持续分享这些内容的办法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe check out Toast and use Toast when they're at restaurants.
turns.zh: 或许可以试试Toast，在餐厅用餐时用Toast支付。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Oh yes, Plug, Toast. Come work with us. We're the best. I get to work with John Cutler. It's phenomenal.
turns.zh: 哦，对，Plug，还有Toast。来我们公司工作吧。我们是最棒的。我能和约翰·卡特勒（John Cutler）共事，这简直太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Legendary, previous guest. Are there roles you're hiring for just for folks that are listening and just like, hey, maybe I should go do that.
turns.zh: 太传奇了，上期嘉宾。有没有适合正在听节目的听众的职位空缺？比如，嘿，或许我该去应聘一下。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: There are always roles that are open. I don't know what the most open roles are right now, but yeah, check it out. It's a great place.
turns.zh: 我们一直有职位空缺。我不知道当前最紧缺的职位是什么，但还是去看看吧。我们公司很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Willing to the careers page.
turns.zh: 欢迎访问我们的招聘页面。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maggie, thank you again so much for being here.
turns.zh: 玛吉，再次非常感谢你能来。

turns.speaker: Maggie Crowley
turns.en: Thank you, Lenny. It was awesome.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，莱尼。这真是太棒了。
